## Questions? We have answers

How is AI visibility measured in Ahrefs Brand Radar?

Brand Radar measures AI visibility by running 457M+ search-backed prompts through AI platforms (AI Overviews, AI Mode, ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini, Copilot) and storing every response. Your visibility is then calculated from [how often your brand is mentioned or cited in those responses, with these key metrics:](https://help.ahrefs.com/articles/11064852-about-brand-radar)

    *   Mentions – how often your brand name appears in AI answer text

    *   Citations – how often AI links to your pages or domains as a source

    *   AI Share of Voice – the percentage of AI responses within your topic set that mention or cite your brand versus competitors

    *   Estimated Impressions – potential visibility weighted by the real search volume behind each prompt

*   What’s the difference between the AI Visibility Index and Custom Prompts?

The AI Visibility Index maps how brands appear across millions of pre-collected AI responses, instantly, with no setup. It’s ideal for benchmarking share of voice and discovering topics you didn’t know AI was answering. It works best for established brands or topics with meaningful search demand, since the index is built on Ahrefs’ keyword database and may have limited coverage for brands with little or no search volume.

[Custom Prompts](https://ahrefs.com/custom-prompts) are specific buyer questions answered by the AI platforms that matter to your pipeline, defined and set up by you, populated with data from the moment you start tracking. Brand Radar runs them on demand as often as daily. They are great if your brand is not well-known, or you have uncommon queries to track.  
*   
How does Ahrefs Brand Radar collect AI visibility data?

Brand Radar builds two distinct kinds of indexes:

    *   Prompt-based indexes (ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini, Copilot, AI Overviews, AI Mode). [Ahrefs takes real queries from its keyword database](https://ahrefs.com/blog/brand-radar-methodology/), expands them into natural questions via People Also Ask and semantic fanout, then runs the resulting 457M+ prompts through each AI platform and stores the responses.

    *   Search-query-based indexes (AI Overviews and AI Mode only). Instead of asking AI a question, these track the keywords that trigger an AI answer inside Google Search, and whether your brand appears in it. They exist only for AI Overviews and AI Mode, because those are the only AI surfaces that show up in Google’s own results.

Question sets are re-tested monthly on a 90-day reporting window. Because both index types derive from real search demand, not synthetic guesses, the visibility metrics reflect what people really ask.

*   
What kind of queries can I track in Ahrefs Brand Radar?

Brand Radar tracks AI visibility across two query types, filterable by platform:

    *   Prompts – long-tail natural-language questions available for ChatGPT, AI Overviews, AI Mode, Gemini, Perplexity, Copilot, and Claude.

    *   Search queries – short queries that triggered an AI answer in Google (via AI Overview or AI Mode). Brand Radar tracks whether your brand appears in it. This type only covers AI Overviews and AI Mode, because they’re the only ones that show up inside Google Search.

*   
Can I backtrack my AI visibility data to my SEO strategy?

Yes. Every prompt in the Index maps back to real search demand, on two levels:

    *   Search demand – the branded keywords behind your mentions, so you can see the actual query volume driving your AI visibility.

    *   Topics – clustered keywords that group related queries, so you can see which high-volume topics trigger AI answers, which pages and domains get cited, and where your content is (or isn’t) feeding AI responses.

Brand Radar also tracks the social channels that influence AI answers (Reddit threads ranking in Google and YouTube).

*   Do I need to set anything up or wait for data to collect?

For the AI Visibility Index, you don’t have to set anything up. You can immediately search any brand, product, or entire category, including historical responses back to 2025, and no domain cap.

If you choose Custom Prompts, you have to configure them yourself. The data starts to accumulate from that point. You can choose the checking cadence from monthly to daily per AI platform.  
*   
How fresh is the data, and which platforms are covered?

The AI Visibility Index covers:

    *   AI Overviews

    *   AI Mode

    *   ChatGPT

    *   Perplexity

    *   Gemini

    *   Copilot

Its question sets are re-tested monthly on a 90-day reporting window (Search Demand refreshes every few days, Web Visibility every few minutes).

Custom Prompts supports all of the above plus Claude. You pick the tracking cadence per platform (daily, weekly, or monthly), so you can spend your checks where freshness matters most. Every paid [Ahrefs plan includes a daily Custom Prompts quota](https://ahrefs.com/custom-prompts) (Lite 5, Standard 10, Advanced 20), with larger check-based packages available.

kept.heading: YOUTUBE INFLUENCERS HAVE AN AI AUDIENCE: WHAT MILLIONS OF CITATION EVENTS REVEAL ABOUT INFLUENCER SPONSORSHIPS (9 MINUTE READ)
kept.blurb: Sponsored YouTube videos can extend their marketing value into AI search when the video is cited, especially through the description text that names the sponsor. The sponsor appeared in 40% of AI answers that cited a sponsored video, compared with 32.3% when the video was not cited, and the lift reached 1.35x on unbranded prompts. Brands should make specific description language part of influencer contracts and track YouTube citations for the prompts that matter to them, rather than treating sponsorship as a view-based channel alone. The opportunity is temporary because YouTube citation rates fell 43% within a month, so citation monitoring needs to be ongoing.

Title: YouTube influencers have an AI audience: What millions of citation events reveal about influencer sponsorships

URL Source: https://scrunch.com/blog/youtube-influencers-have-an-ai-audience-influencer-sponsorships/

Published Time: 2026-09-10T00:00:00.000Z

Markdown Content:
**TLDR:**

*   When AI cites a YouTube video with a description that names a sponsor, that sponsor gets mentioned in the answer about 1.24x more often (40% of the time versus 32.3%). On unbranded category prompts, the lift grows to 1.35x.
*   The effect lives primarily in the four platforms most likely to cite YouTube: Google AI Mode, Google AI Overviews, Perplexity, and Gemini.
*   YouTube citations fade by more than 40% within a month, but the sponsor-named-if-cited effect remains strong over the same time period.

YouTube is increasingly spotlighted as a top citation source in AI search.

[Our own research](https://scrunch.com/blog/reddit-paradox-industry-breakdown-of-most-cited-ai-sources) previously found that it’s a strong cross-industry generalist: YouTube popped up as a top 10 source across automotive, retail, technology, and other industries.

Whether or not it’s uniquely influential for _your_ business depends on your category, your niche within it, and the prompts you’re tracking, but there’s no denying that YouTube is a powerful lever for brands.

Not just in terms of AI answers, but also in terms of sponsored content (it’s estimated that [brands will spend approximately $3B-$6B on YouTube influencers](https://influencerfee.com/blog/youtube-influencer-statistics-2025/) in 2026).

Which got us thinking: When a brand pays a YouTuber to mention them in a video, and that video later shows up as a source in an AI answer, does the sponsor benefit as well?

We wanted to understand how sponsored YouTube content travels into AI answers when videos enter retrieval, so we measured three months’ worth of multi-AI assistant search data (May 2026 to July 2026) covering thousands of sponsored videos, hundreds of brands, and millions of citation events.

You can dig into our findings below.

The big takeaway? Sponsored YouTube content can boost your brand even after human viewers hit pause.

**What do we mean by sponsored content?**

This study is specifically about sponsorship information reflected in YouTube video descriptions ("thanks to Brand X for sponsoring"-style mentions in the text under a video), not pre-roll/mid-roll ads or other YouTube monetization channels.

![Image 1](https://cdn.sanity.io/images/3lyosn52/production/95792feb374ce1647bb81079ed0f78760949e67b-4000x2500.png)

To cut to the chase: Yes, sponsored YouTube videos can carry sponsor names into AI answers.

We analyzed the same question asked of the same AI assistant on different occasions. When the answer cited a sponsored video, the sponsor got named about 40% of the time. When it didn’t, about 32.3%. That’s a 1.24x lift.

The effect is even stronger for unbranded category prompts. When someone asks an AI a question and doesn’t name the brand, and the AI cites the brand’s sponsored video, sponsors see a 1.35x lift.

It’s worth being clear that this is what happens in answers where AI picks a sponsored video as a source. It’s not what a sponsorship deal is worth in AI search automatically. Whether YouTube pays off this way for a given campaign depends on how many relevant questions people are asking and how often a video gets cited.

We ran our analysis with an unrelated brand swapped in for the sponsor (a placebo brand). The effect disappeared, so this isn't just AI answers naming more brands whenever they cite a commercial (aka brand-heavy) video.

What we can't separate is payment from placement. A brand that’s name sits high in YouTube description text, is repeated, and is next to a discount code might get a similar bump without a dollar changing hands. Sponsorship is a reliable way to get your name written that way, but it may not be the only way.

While the effect is real, it’s also platform-specific and, due to citation decay, somewhat temporary.

The lift is concentrated across the four AI platforms most likely to cite YouTube to begin with: Google AI Mode, Google AI Overviews, Perplexity, and Gemini. Platforms like ChatGPT and Microsoft Copilot rarely cite YouTube.

Google AI Mode had a ~30% YouTube citation rate, followed by Google AI Overviews at ~27%, Perplexity at ~15%, Gemini at ~4%, Copilot at ~0.5%, and ChatGPT at ~0.3%.

**A note on the AI assistants we measured**

Our research is based on AI answers that we could measure in the same way across our three-month window. While Claude, Grok, and Meta AI search the web and cite sources, for various reasons (e.g., answering too often from training versus real-time retrieval), they didn’t qualify for this study.

![Image 2](https://cdn.sanity.io/images/3lyosn52/production/adf249a50cc6926cc762a1aa7863fc813ad2c15c-4000x2500.png)

Google’s AI Mode and AI Overviews were the heaviest carriers of the effect. YouTube citations resulted in a 1.28x lift in brand mentions in Google AI Mode and a 1.22x lift in AI Overviews. Gemini and Perplexity had smaller per-citation lifts, coming in at 1.08x and 1.07x, respectively.

**A note on shifting retrieval pipelines**

Around August 12, 2026, Perplexity stopped citing YouTube almost entirely. Over the same period, YouTube's share of citations across Google's AI surfaces went up. ChatGPT and Copilot still rarely cite YouTube.

Remember: Retrieval pipelines can change under you. Use a tool like Scrunch to see how citations are performing right now for the prompts you care about.

We also found that YouTube citations fade by roughly 43% within a month, going from an 18.4% citation rate to 10.5%.

The payoff holds up much better than the citations do. When a sponsored video _does_ get cited, the sponsor still gets named about as often as before: That rate drops only about 12%, from 57.3% to 50.3%. However, fewer citations means fewer chances for sponsor brands to benefit.

This timeline is based on the first time the AI ecosystem started citing the video in our data. It’s not the day the sponsorship was filmed or paid for—sponsorship was already in place from upload. What we measured was the moment the sponsored video entered AI retrieval and what happened next.

**Why do YouTube citations fade within a few weeks?**

We don't know with certainty. The most likely explanations are retrieval recency (newer videos rotate in to displace older ones), AI ecosystem changes (the AI assistants update their indexes and rankings frequently), or topical drift (the topic cluster's prompts shift over time). The fade shows up broadly across the sponsorships we tracked, not in a handful of them, so it’s not a one-off pattern.

While a one-month cliff may sound fleeting, keep in mind that all citations come with a countdown clock.

[Our study with Stacker](https://scrunch.com/blog/half-life-of-ai-citations) revealed that, for the average citation source, citation activity drops by half in about 4-5 weeks. Source half-life is dependent on the AI platform, the industry, and the source itself, but relatively quick shifts in citation activity are normal.

At any rate, our research suggests that YouTube influencer sponsorships may create value outside of the human view count in the form of AI-answer exposure.

The point: For creators and YouTube partners, AI citations can become part of the sponsorship value story they offer to brands. And for brands and the agencies that serve them, campaign reporting can track whether sponsored videos are getting cited in AI answers.

![Image 3](https://cdn.sanity.io/images/3lyosn52/production/468119e727e49fb5afdbe798f2ccb9025fc196eb-4000x2500.png)

Imagine you run influencer marketing at a wireless-speaker company.

You pay a tech YouTuber to mention your products in a video about home audio equipment. The video’s description says, "Thanks to Brand X for sponsoring this video. Get 10% off at brandx.com/creator."

A couple of weeks later, someone asks one of the major YouTube-citing AI assistants something like: "What are the best wireless speakers under $300 for an apartment with spotty Wi-Fi?"

The AI assistant searches, picks a few sources to cite, and includes your sponsored video as one of them.

When the AI writes its answer, your brand gets a name-check about 40% of the time (versus only about 32% of the time when the same AI assistant, asked the same question on a different occasion, doesn’t cite the video).

Big picture: A brand that sponsors a YouTube video isn’t just buying an influencer ad anymore. They’re also potentially buying more visibility in a second, increasingly crucial channel: AI search.

**Is the mention just because the sponsor was already topically relevant?**

This is partly handled by design in our measurement. The cross-sectional headline holds the same prompt and the same AI assistant constant, so any reason the brand was already topically relevant for that prompt would also push the control side up (it doesn't go into the "lift").

That said, there are two things we can't fully rule out. We can't separate "the brand paid for this" from "the brand's name sits high in the description, repeated, next to a discount code." A brand written that way without paying might get a similar bump. And if a brand happened to be in the news the same week its video started getting cited, our design wouldn't cleanly separate that either.

![Image 4](https://cdn.sanity.io/images/3lyosn52/production/b6090916e3f78dd71d8342bf968c51f33d4b175a-4000x2500.png)

We’re not saying every brand should run out and start sponsoring YouTube influencers to juice their AI search performance.

But here are some tips for how to act on this information, whether you’re running YouTube influencer campaigns today or thinking about it.

### Figure out how important YouTube is to your prompts

“Helpful for AI search” doesn’t necessarily mean “helpful for you.”

YouTube may not matter all that much for your particular prompt set. Use a platform like Scrunch to find out how influential YouTube is for the prompts you’re tracking.

If YouTube doesn’t move the needle for the prompts you care about, that doesn’t mean it’s a bad investment for marketing outside of AI search. It just means you shouldn’t count on it to pull double duty.

### Lean on the description box

The lift we found lives in the YouTube description box. Getting your name into the text under the video is the part that we can show increases brand mentions.

So make description text part of the deal with any influencer you work with, not an afterthought.

When you brief your YouTuber, spell out exactly how your brand should appear in the description. The voiceover sells the humans watching. The text sells the AI reading.

### Focus on unbranded prompts

The lift is bigger when your brand isn’t the obvious answer. If someone typed your name into AI search to begin with, AI was almost certainly going to talk about you anyway.

Unbranded prompts are where AI is genuinely shopping. A cited video that names you can tip the response your way.

And remember: Focusing on unbranded prompts is a good practice well beyond YouTube. You want to make sure AI answers about your brand are positive and accurate, yes, but first you have to make sure AI mentions you at all.

### Don’t set and forget your citation strategy

YouTube or not, citations are on a timer.

That means the sources shaping AI answers today may not be the ones shaping them next month. A video, article, or page that's driving your mentions right now can get displaced as newer content rotates in and platforms update their indexes.

So treat citation tracking as ongoing, not one-and-done. Learn which sources feed the prompts that matter most to your business, watch for when those citations shift, and move fast when an important one drops out.

### Don’t sleep on your own website

Third-party citations are critical, but owned content is another piece of the puzzle.

Your website is the one source you control completely. The problem is that most sites are built for humans, not AI. If AI can't read it, it won't cite it.

Invest in tooling that helps you [optimize your site for AI retrievability and citability](https://scrunch.com/blog/site-diagnostics-always-on-action-plan-for-winning-ai-search/). Whether the issues are technical or editorial, you need to know what to fix to make your site as easy as possible for AI to consume.

Every sponsored YouTube video has two audiences now: the humans who watch it and the AI bots that read it.

You're already paying for the first. Scrunch helps you find out if you’re benefitting from the second.

Track and win the sources that shape AI answers. Start a [7-day free trial](https://app.scrunchai.com/sign-up/?ph=01a0a202-96a9-7dd3-8ff4-0bff210051e0&__hstc=165127776.b8370c66174c89310250ef55607cee35.1789424476134.1789424476134.1789424476134.1&__hssc=165127776.1.1789424476135&__hsfp=c9ec2167225d0fbea51f1728162c37bf) or [get in touch](https://scrunchai.com/book/?__hstc=165127776.b8370c66174c89310250ef55607cee35.1789424476134.1789424476134.1789424476134.1&__hssc=165127776.1.1789424476135&__hsfp=c9ec2167225d0fbea51f1728162c37bf) to see how Scrunch can help you optimize your approach to AI citations.

* * *

**How we tested this:**

*   We checked it two ways, using data from May 2026 to July 2026.
*   First, we looked at the same question asked of the same AI assistant many times over. Sometimes the answer cited the sponsored video and sometimes it didn't, so we compared those two groups. Holding the question and the assistant fixed is what keeps the comparison fair:Aany reason a brand was already a likely answer to that question pushes up both sides, so it doesn't show up as lift.
*   Secondly, we followed videos through the month after an AI assistant first cited them, tracking two things separately: how often the video was still getting cited, and how often the sponsor got named in the answers that cited it. That's what tells us how long the payoff lasts.

**What we counted:**

*   The sponsor's name in the answer text, not coupon codes, URLs, or the sponsor's own phrasing. Whether the brand name shows up is the whole outcome.
*   Sponsorship language in the video description. We read the text under the video, never the audio.

**What to keep in mind:**

*   **Observational, not experimental:** We measure correlation in carefully stratified subsets. Nobody randomized which videos got sponsored.
*   **Conditional on a citation event:** The lift only fires when the video is cited. What a campaign is worth also depends on how often that happens, which is a separate question.
*   **The citations fade, the payoff mostly doesn't:** Over the month after a video's first citation, how often it's still cited falls by more than 40%. The rate at which the sponsor gets named when the video is cited holds about 88% of where it started.
*   **Scope:** This is about the AI surfaces that cite YouTube. Google AI Mode, Google AI Overviews, Perplexity, and Gemini carry essentially all of the YouTube citations we see, and we measured all four the same way across the full three months. ChatGPT and Microsoft Copilot are in the numbers as the contrast: They almost never cite YouTube.
*   **Sponsor detection is narrow:** Under 1% of cited YouTube videos carry explicit sponsorship language naming a brand in the description. Sponsorships disclosed only in the voiceover are invisible to us, and we can't say which way that tilts the headline.
*   **Mention rates were already rising before citation:** In the three weeks before a video's first citation, sponsor mention rates were climbing by roughly as much as the jump that follows. A simple before-and-after would credit the citation with a rise that was already underway, which is why we report per-citation figures instead.
*   **Placebo brand:** We ran the same analysis looking for an unrelated brand's name in place of the sponsor's, and the association disappeared. That rules out AI answers simply naming more brands whenever they cite a commercial video. It doesn't separate paying from placement.
*   **"Unbranded" means the prompt doesn't name the sponsor:** On prompts that do name it, the sponsor appears in about 99.9% of answers whether or not the video is cited. There's no headroom left, which is why the 1.35x belongs to prompts that don't name you.
*   **What this design can't show:** whether paying is what does it, or whether having your name high in a description next to a discount code would do the same on its own. The description box is the only part of a video we read. And nothing here speaks to clicks or sales.
*   **External validity:** These results describe the AI ecosystem from May to July 2026, and it keeps moving. Around August 12, Perplexity stopped citing YouTube almost entirely. Read the levels as a snapshot and the mechanism as the finding.

kept.blurb: Shopping ad CTRs are rising while impressions are falling across thousands of campaigns, with clicks relatively flat or slightly down. One hypothesis is that Google's AI Overviews are appearing on queries less likely to generate ad clicks, leaving Shopping ads for higher-intent searches. The data doesn't prove AI Overviews are causing the decline, but advertisers should look beyond CTR and track impressions, clicks, and overall traffic to understand whether performance is actually improving.

kept.heading: DON'T RECOMMEND YOUR MOST EXPENSIVE OPTION (2 MINUTE READ)
kept.blurb: Increase sales by labeling a mid-priced product as “recommended” instead of your most expensive option. In eight experiments involving more than 6,200 participants, sales of a recommended cafe drink increased 58% when a pricier option was added, while sales were unchanged without the recommendation. Consumers appear more receptive to recommendations when the suggested product is cheaper because the brand seems less motivated by profit. Use objective badges such as “Bestseller” when recommending a premium product, and test this pricing tactic on comparable products where customers can easily evaluate the price difference.

Title: Don’t recommend your most expensive option

*   [Make your discounts a bit harder to get](https://app.sciencesays.com/p/make-your-discounts-a-bit-harder-to-get)

**Topic**: Pricing | Ecommerce

**For**: B2C, can be tested for B2B

**Research date**: July 2026

**Universities**: Nanyang Technological University, Indiana University Bloomington

#### 📈**Recommendation**

Don’t label as “recommended” the most expensive product in your lineup (e.g. a premium package). Instead, recommend a cheaper alternative (e.g. a mid-tier priced one, one you know sells very well).

People will be much more likely to choose it, increasing your overall sales and likely your profits.

If the most expensive option is the best fit, give an objective reason for why you’re recommending it (e.g. “Our Bestseller” or “XYZ Judge’s Choice”).

![Image 2](https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,format=auto,onerror=redirect,quality=80/uploads/asset/file/b44fb54d-bf30-4952-b82a-e40a66ee821a/Insight__339.png?t=1788256892)

#### **🎓 Findings**

*   As part of a series of 8 experiments with over 6,200 participants, researchers found that:

    *   Sales for a recommended drink at a South Korean cafe increased 58% when a more expensive option was also available, while both were equal without the recommendation

    *   People were 24% more interested in buying when the recommended option was the cheapest one, and 8% less interested when it was the most expensive one

    *   Adding an “Amazon’s choice” label increased people choosing a product by 159% when it was the second-most-expensive option, but by 357% when a competitor’s prices made it the third-cheapest option

#### 🧠**Why it works**

*   We assume companies are [trying to influence us](https://doi.org/10.1086/209380?utm_source=sciencesays&utm_medium=referral&utm_campaign=don-t-recommend-your-most-expensive-option) when labelling something as "recommended".

*   When they recommend the most expensive option, we assume they're just trying to make more profit and [judge them differently](https://doi.org/10.1086/314309?utm_source=sciencesays&utm_medium=referral&utm_campaign=don-t-recommend-your-most-expensive-option).

*   If the recommended option is at a lower price, we're more likely to accept the recommendation because we don’t see an ulterior motive.

*   This can look like the [decoy effect](https://doi.org/10.1086/208899?utm_source=sciencesays&utm_medium=referral&utm_campaign=don-t-recommend-your-most-expensive-option), where adding another option changes what people choose, but differs because adding a more expensive option only helped when the cheaper product was also recommended.

#### ✋**Limitations**

*   The study looked at items where the price was visible and could be compared (e.g. similar boxes of pasta). It’s likely the effect doesn’t work if there are clear differences between the products (e.g. 1 pasta is organic and 1 is wholewheat).

*   The effect is likely weaker for products where people rely heavily on recommendations (e.g. choosing a hotel for vacation or buying a car).

#### 👀**Real-life example**

Bedding and towels brand Cozy Earth highlights certain options to nudge customers towards those items.

![Image 3](https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,format=auto,onerror=redirect,quality=80/uploads/asset/file/ce0e0934-3c1c-41aa-a6c8-59d785f2c854/339_Example.png?t=1788257619)

❌**Issue:**The towels marked as “Selling Fast” are more expensive than the other options.

✅**Solution:**

*   Recommend a cheaper option with the “Selling Fast” badge instead of the most expensive option.

*   Add a badge with details to justify the price difference between the recommended set and other sets (e.g. “Ultra-soft fabric”).

*   Highlight features of the towel sets instead of the price, and test [showing the price later](https://app.sciencesays.com/p/when-to-show-vs-hide-prices), after someone clicks on a specific towel set.

*   Use [rounded prices](https://app.sciencesays.com/p/rounded-vs-unrounded-prices) (e.g. $360 instead of $364), as these work better for items bought for pleasure or luxury, as compared to utility.

#### 📖**Research**

_Remember: This is_ _a new_ _scientific discovery. In the future it will probably be better understood and could even be proven wrong (that’s_[how science works](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scientific_method?utm_source=sciencesays&utm_medium=referral&utm_campaign=don-t-recommend-your-most-expensive-option)_). It may also not be generalizable to your situation. If it’s a risky change, always test it on a small scale before rolling it out widely._

Title: The Legacy Brand De-Aging Playbook

URL Source: https://thebrandblueprint.substack.com/p/the-legacy-brand-de-aging-playbook

Published Time: 2026-09-10T14:42:14+00:00

Markdown Content:
[![Image 1](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!KK1d!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F6dacd6e0-d7e6-4c04-93ac-97c5bf1e32a0_1920x1080.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!KK1d!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F6dacd6e0-d7e6-4c04-93ac-97c5bf1e32a0_1920x1080.png)

Happy Thursday!

I hope everyone had a great long weekend and is surviving a 4 day work week.

I spend a lot of my time researching and talking about challenger brands. They are obviously building some of the coolest products, have some of the best marketing, and are bringing some real innovation to the table.

But I think it’s time I look at the other side.

How do legacy brands stay relevant, or almost “anti-age,” to younger audiences?

Building a brand that can adapt and last is almost harder at times than building a challenger brand. You have decades of brand recognition and loyal customers you do not want to lose, while also needing to convince a new generation that the brand is still relevant to them.

So let’s break down some of my favorite legacy brand comebacks and the different strategies they used to get there.

We are helping subscription brands increase their subscription revenue with our subscription agent and operating team. Helping brands boost their subscription rates by 2-10%. Click **[here](https://calendly.com/avidai/chat-with-brooke-yoakam)** to book a call with me to get a full deep dive for free.

[![Image 2](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!fNmy!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F9ab12e71-3ef3-4461-bd2b-e47030bfa2a8_1920x1080.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!fNmy!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F9ab12e71-3ef3-4461-bd2b-e47030bfa2a8_1920x1080.png)

For this article, I’m defining a legacy brand as a company that has been around long enough to have an established identity, customer base, and cultural perception.

That history can be an incredible advantage. People already know your name, recognize your products, and have some relationship with the brand.

But it can also become baggage.

The things that made a brand iconic 20 years ago can eventually make it feel dated. And unlike a challenger brand starting with a blank slate, a legacy brand cannot change everything without risking the customers and recognition it already has.

**The challenge is figuring out what needs to change and what is actually worth keeping.**

So let’s dive into the brands that handled this challenge correctly.

[![Image 3](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!JLaM!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fb2378d53-f53e-41ac-8ea6-ab04e1351f2f_1522x742.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!JLaM!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fb2378d53-f53e-41ac-8ea6-ab04e1351f2f_1522x742.png)

Sometimes making a brand feel younger means letting it grow up. Customers change, and brands can become relevant again by evolving with their lives.

**[Abercrombie & Fitch](https://go.shopmy.us/p-85538769)** went from teen mall culture, shirtless models, dark stores, and exclusivity to wedding guest dresses, tailored workwear, elevated basics, and more inclusive fits.

Rather than trying to recreate the Abercrombie of the early 2000s, the brand grew up alongside the people who once shopped there.

**Why it works**

Abercrombie already had awareness. What it needed was a new reason for those customers to shop again.

By designing around the lives its former teenage customers have now, the brand was able to turn familiarity into an advantage instead of starting over with an entirely new audience.

**Thoughts to ask for your brand**

*   Has your original customer changed faster than your brand has?

*   What does that customer need from you at their current stage of life?

[![Image 4](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!SmCS!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fae30ea74-ddb9-47da-83f0-6ee1a5901bcf_1564x736.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!SmCS!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fae30ea74-ddb9-47da-83f0-6ee1a5901bcf_1564x736.png)

Legacy brands do not always need new brand codes. Sometimes they need to make the ones they already own culturally relevant again.

**[Gap](https://go.shopmy.us/p-85538820)** had become associated with generic mall basics, constant promotions, and very little cultural point of view. But its recent comeback has returned to things that were historically part of the brand: denim, music, dance, and culturally relevant talent.

Campaigns with artists like KATSEYE have taken those familiar Gap codes and introduced them through the people and platforms younger consumers care about now.

**Why it works**

Gap is not pretending to be a new brand.

It is taking assets it has authentically owned for decades and changing the context around them. That makes the comeback feel like an evolution of Gap rather than a legacy company desperately trying to act young.

**Thoughts to ask for your brand**

*   Which parts of your history still have cultural value?

*   Could you modernize how those brand codes show up instead of replacing them?

[![Image 5](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!XY1f!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fbc5c536e-80f2-4758-849c-dfce14d6130b_1626x734.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!XY1f!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fbc5c536e-80f2-4758-849c-dfce14d6130b_1626x734.png)

Changing the perception of an entire brand can sometimes start with one product.

**[Coach](https://go.shopmy.us/p-85538709)** had become heavily associated with outlets, logo-heavy bags, and a version of accessible luxury that younger consumers did not necessarily aspire to own.

Instead of trying to reinvent everything at once, Coach created desirable hero products that gave a new generation an entry point into the brand. Bags like the Tabby helped reposition Coach as attainable luxury that could still feel fashionable and culturally relevant.

**Why it works**

One desirable product can become the reason someone reconsiders a brand they had previously written off.

Once younger consumers start wanting the hero product, that new perception can spread to the rest of the assortment. You do not necessarily need to change everything to change what the brand means.

**Thoughts to ask for your brand**

*   Is there one product that could change how customers perceive everything else you sell?

*   What would your gateway product look like for a younger customer?

[![Image 6](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!E-g_!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Ff27e553b-bde7-4811-b3bf-ff818101be09_2102x894.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!E-g_!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Ff27e553b-bde7-4811-b3bf-ff818101be09_2102x894.png)

Sometimes the next version of a legacy brand is discovered by the customer before it is discovered by the company.

For decades, **[Stanley 1913](https://go.shopmy.us/p-85538845)** was known for durable thermoses associated with outdoor use and blue-collar workers. Then a completely different customer started embracing the Quencher.

Stanley listened. The brand leaned into colorful drops, new distribution, scarcity, and collectability, turning hydration into something closer to a fashion accessory.

**Why it works**

Stanley did not decide from the top down that it suddenly wanted to become a lifestyle brand for women.

Customers showed the company an entirely different meaning for an existing product, and Stanley was willing to build around that behavior. Sometimes the smartest repositioning strategy is paying attention to who is already pulling your brand somewhere new.

**Thoughts to ask for your brand**

*   Is an unexpected customer already using your product differently?

*   What behavior is happening organically that you could build around?

[![Image 7](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!HZ0l!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F89d99e3b-274a-45d2-ae19-b8b03d0b8cf9_1724x808.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!HZ0l!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F89d99e3b-274a-45d2-ae19-b8b03d0b8cf9_1724x808.png)

Scale can become a disadvantage when every customer gets exactly the same experience.

For years, **[Barnes & Noble](https://www.barnesandnoble.com/)** operated much more like a traditional big-box retailer. Its comeback has involved giving individual booksellers and stores more control over what they stock, display, and recommend based on their local customers.

Instead of every Barnes & Noble feeling identical, stores can behave more like local bookstores inside a national brand.

**Why it works**

The people closest to the customer often understand changing tastes faster than headquarters does.

Giving stores more autonomy makes the experience feel curated and creates room to respond to local interests and cultural trends without waiting for one corporate strategy to dictate everything.

**Thoughts to ask for your brand**

*   Who inside your company is actually closest to changing customer behavior?

*   Are your brand guidelines creating consistency or preventing cultural relevance?

[![Image 8](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!rw6A!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F2e586d0a-b361-42eb-946c-90487cf38344_1660x788.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!rw6A!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F2e586d0a-b361-42eb-946c-90487cf38344_1660x788.png)

Sometimes the thing making a brand feel old eventually becomes the exact thing that makes it interesting again.

**[New Balance](https://go.shopmy.us/p-85538934)** spent years with a reputation for practical “dad shoes.” Instead of completely abandoning that identity, the brand leaned into retro silhouettes, fashion collaborations, and the product heritage it already had as culture moved toward that aesthetic.

What once looked outdated suddenly looked cool.

**Why it works**

New Balance did not have to manufacture retro credibility. It already had decades of it.

When culture shifted, the brand’s history became an advantage that newer competitors could imitate aesthetically but could not recreate authentically.

**Thoughts to ask for your brand**

*   Is something you consider outdated actually becoming culturally relevant again?

*   What do you authentically own that newer competitors can only imitate?

[![Image 9](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Jkkv!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F3aec8ccd-9536-4798-a3d2-d691da13b675_1696x742.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Jkkv!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F3aec8ccd-9536-4798-a3d2-d691da13b675_1696x742.png)

When an entire category moves in one direction, the old experience can suddenly become the countertrend.

As restaurants moved toward fast casual, delivery, and increasingly expensive meals, **[Chili’s](https://www.chilis.com/)** leaned into what it already did well: value, indulgent food, booths, drinks, and the fun of actually going out to eat.

Products like the Triple Dipper also gave that experience a new life on social media, turning a classic casual dining meal into something people wanted to film, customize, and talk about.

**Why it works**

Chili’s did not try to become a trendy fast-casual restaurant to attract younger customers.

It made the parts of the brand that once felt dated feel fun again. In a category full of expensive takeout and delivery, the traditional casual dining experience can suddenly feel like the alternative.

**Thoughts to ask for your brand**

*   Has the rest of your category moved far enough that your old positioning now feels different again?

*   Could something customers once considered dated become your point of differentiation?

Legacy brands have something challenger brands would spend millions trying to build: awareness, history, recognizable products, and years of customer memories.

The problem is that history only becomes valuable if the next generation sees a reason to care about it.

The brands doing this best are not erasing their past or pretending to be startups. They are figuring out which parts of their history still have value and giving a new generation a reason to interpret them differently.

Have a great rest of your week!

kept.heading: GOOGLE LAUNCHES TOOL TO CHECK WHETHER ADS ACTUALLY INCREASE SALES (2 MINUTE READ)
kept.blurb: Google released an open-source tool that tests whether an ad actually caused a sale, not just which platform claims credit for one. GeoX works by comparing regions where a campaign keeps running against regions where it's paused or given more budget, then measuring how sales in each group differ from what historical data would have predicted anyway. It can track spend across platforms beyond Google's own and combine online and offline sales in the same test. It plugs into Google's existing Meridian measurement software, so the results can also refine how a budget gets split across channels.

kept.blurb: Amazon has spent months locking AI shopping agents like Claude and Gemini out of its own storefront while building its own AI shopping tools, then quietly became ChatGPT's top retail advertiser between April and August instead. It's now opening that same access to other brands that already buy through its demand-side platform, letting them run ads inside ChatGPT conversations too. Campaigns are still set up and managed inside Amazon's own systems, while OpenAI's ad system keeps control over which ad actually gets served.

# Amazon gives OpenAI’s ad business a boost, letting its advertisers into ChatGPT

Published Thu, Sep 10 2026 9:01 AM EDT Updated Thu, Sep 10 2026 11:25 AM EDT

![Image 8: thumbnail](https://image.cnbcfm.com/api/v1/image/106198914-157185168879320191011-img_3215.jpg?v=1571851773&w=60&h=60&ffmt=webp)

*   Amazon is partnering with OpenAI to let select U.S. brands run ads in ChatGPT.
*   The pilot could give a boost to OpenAI’s burgeoning advertising business, which recently reached a $1 billion annualized revenue run rate.
*   Amazon has been hesitant to open its sprawling webstore to external AI platforms.

[Amazon](https://www.cnbc.com/quotes/AMZN/) on Thursday announced it’s partnering with [OpenAI](https://www.cnbc.com/quotes/OPENAI.FG/) to let its advertisers run ads in ChatGPT, starting with select brands in the U.S.

It marks a vote of confidence from the world’s largest online retailer in OpenAI’s burgeoning ad business, which recently reached a [$1 billion](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/08/31/open-ai-chatgpt-ads-revenue.html) annualized revenue run rate. OpenAI started selling sponsored placements in ChatGPT in the U.S. [in February](https://openai.com/index/testing-ads-in-chatgpt/), starting with retailers like [Best Buy](https://www.cnbc.com/quotes/BBY/) and [Williams-Sonoma](https://www.cnbc.com/quotes/WSM/).

Amazon has [heavily restricted](https://www.cnbc.com/2025/12/24/amazon-faces-a-dilemma-fight-ai-shopping-agents-or-join-them.html) access to its sprawling webstore from artificial intelligence platforms like ChatGPT, [Anthropic](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/09/01/anthropic-data-retention.html)’s Claude and [Google](https://www.cnbc.com/quotes/GOOGL/)’s Gemini, while investing in its own [AI shopping tools](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/05/13/amazon-ditches-rufus-ai-chatbot-in-favor-of-alexa-shopping-agent.html). But in recent months, Amazon began quietly [buying ads](https://www.businessinsider.com/amazon-first-chatgpt-ads-ai-strategy-openai-data-2026-6) on ChatGPT, and it became the top retail company advertising on the platform between April and August, according to data from market intelligence firm Sensor Tower.

By letting brands that advertise on Amazon run ads in ChatGPT, the Andy Jassy-led giant is acknowledging that the platform has become an important marketing channel. OpenAI said in February that ChatGPT reached [900 million](https://openai.com/index/scaling-ai-for-everyone/) weekly active users.

Amazon said in a blog post that conversational ad formats like those that appear in AI chatbots are the “fastest growing engagement opportunity” for brands to reach new and existing customers.

“With Access to ChatGPT Ads, advertisers can now extend their campaigns further into where their customers are actively spending time in conversational chat platforms,” Chris Conetta, director of omnichannel supply at Amazon’s demand-side advertising platform, said in a statement.

Ad campaigns are set up and managed by Amazon, while OpenAI’s ads system controls all ad delivery decisions, an Amazon spokesperson said. Ad units will appear as text or images beneath ChatGPT responses, they added.

OpenAI [has said](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/20001047-ads-in-chatgpt) ads are served below the end of a ChatGPT response and are “clearly labeled” as sponsored. For example, if a shopper is looking for marathon training tips in ChatGPT, an ad for running shoes sold on Amazon could be shown in results.

Delta Vacations, the airline’s vacation packages service, is among the companies participating in the trial, according to Amazon’s blog post.

Title: Some companies are using ads to influence AI agents

URL Source: https://www.marketingbrew.com/stories/optimizing-for-ai-agents-time-magazine-wayfair-strategy

Published Time: 2026-09-08T10:00:00.000Z

Markdown Content:
It’s no secret that agents are slowly taking over the internet. Automated traffic across the internet increased almost eight times [faster than human activity](https://www.marketingbrew.com/stories/bot-internet-brands) last year, according to a March report from cybersecurity company Human Security.

But how is a brand to influence them?

As agentic infrastructure continues to develop and as some consumers begin deploying agents to shop or perform other tasks, companies across industries are not only grappling with optimizing their websites for agents but are trying to figure out how to advertise to them. Many brands are thinking beyond just [answer engine optimization](https://www.marketingbrew.com/stories/2025/08/08/how-genai-is-changing-the-seo-marketing-playbook-with-ai-overviews) (AEO) and are working on how to engage directly with agents to drive sales or impact how the agents perceive them, according to executives we spoke to.

“[Agents are] still emerging as a channel,” Fiona Tan, Wayfair’s chief technology officer, told Marketing Brew. “We want to just make sure we’re keeping very close to how consumers are changing their behavior and then reacting as quickly as possible, and in some cases, proactively providing that information.”

## High time

Advertising to agents is top of mind at the publisher Time magazine, as the number of days where it sees more bot traffic than human traffic to its site is increasing, according to Mark Howard, the publication’s chief operating officer. He [cited data](https://www.businessinsider.com/ads-ai-agents-marketing-industry-debate-2026-8?utm_source=chatgpt.com) from Ally Bank showing that consumers who came to the brand from AI referrals tended to have a higher conversion rate and were further down the funnel by the time they got to the brand, which he said makes them an attractive opportunity for its advertising partners.

Advertising to agents directly is one way brands can promote messaging about their products and potentially mitigate incorrect information that AI models may be propagating about them, Howard explained. To capitalize on those opportunities, Time is [partnering](https://digiday.com/media/time-has-started-serving-ads-to-ai-agents/) with ad-tech platform Mobian to run Agent Ads, an ad format [designed](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/jonahgoodhart_we-just-served-what-we-believe-is-the-worlds-share-7488646009657671680-Z2on/) to be readable to agents.

How do Agent Ads work? Howard broke down an Agent Ad showcasing Ally that was running on Time’s site. Time reroutes agents to a “markdown” page containing metadata and identification of the sponsored ad; the agent is then exposed to brand-verified facts and other core ad information, like, in Ally’s case, its founding date and the fact that it is a financial services company. The page closes out with information on where the content of the ad came from, and a disclosure that the ad has concluded. After all that, the agent can then access the actual webpage itself.

Get marketing news you'll actually want to read

Marketing Brew informs marketing pros of the latest on brand strategy, social media, and ad tech via our weekday newsletter, virtual events, marketing conferences, and digital guides.

These agent-specific ads are served to Time’s “allow list” of about 70 agents and bots that are allowed to crawl the site.

“We know as these AI agents come to the site, they’re scraping the page, they’re retaining the information from the page, and oftentimes they’re storing a lot of that information for the ability to either be presented in that moment or in the future without having to necessarily come back to the page and scrape it again,” Howard said. “It’s about getting those brand facts into that knowledge layer of the AI.”

## In the details

It goes beyond influencing agents through ads itself. Optimizing one’s site is key to attracting agents to a brand’s page to crawl it in the first place. While agentic traffic to Wayfair is still “pretty nascent,” Tan said, the company is continuing to add attributes, the information merchants use to describe their products, to provide agents with more information to make recommendations in response to user queries. Wayfair has also been involved in the infrastructure buildout for agentic commerce, partnering with Google as part of a [Universal Commerce Protocol](https://www.marketingbrew.com/stories/2026/01/16/agentic-ai-announcements-ces-nrf) that aims to streamline e-commerce activities.

While some brands are already thinking about advertising to agents, many are still figuring out AEO and how to appear more visible to AI platforms. Tech companies continue to churn out related solutions; in June, Adobe debuted Adobe Brand Visibility, an enterprise platform that aggregates data, including agent traffic data, to help brands see how models are crawling their sites and optimize their online presence. In August, Cloudflare released its AEO Visibility Dashboard, which helps brands understand if and how AI assistants recommend their products to consumers.

Title: How Starface Made Pimple Patches Cool: The Complete Marketing Strategy

URL Source: https://www.marketergems.com/p/starface-marketing-strategy-deep-dive

Published Time: 2026-09-10T11:00:00.000Z

Markdown Content:
Howdy, Marketer!

For decades, the skincare industry built its entire economic engine on a simple, cruel psychological principle: **hide your flaws**.

If you woke up with a massive breakout, the market offered you flesh-toned concealers, harsh gels that smelled like a swimming pool, or skin-matching hydrocolloid dots. Oof.

Acne is often perceived as a personal failure, something to be **sanitized**, **hidden**, and **erased** before you step out the door.

Then, in 2019, Julie Schott and Brian Bordainick looked at that exact same physical real estate - a bright red pimple in the middle of a teenager's cheek - and asked: _what if, instead of hiding it, we made people want to show it off_?

They took a cheap, functional medical product and turned acne treatment into a badge of honor.

That led to the creation of **Starface**. They changed the context without changing the core utility.

[![Image 1](https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,quality=80,format=auto,onerror=redirect/uploads/asset/file/5dbbd539-085f-43f5-af6d-aae17b4519c3/idDZf_yses_logos.png?t=1788971038)](https://starface.world/?utm_campaign=how-starface-made-pimple-patches-cool-the-complete-marketing-strategy&utm_medium=referral&utm_source=www.marketergems.com)

## Today's Treasure Trove

##### advertisement

## Empanada | Drive B2B Pipeline By Activating Your Team On LinkedIn

[![Image 2](https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,quality=80,format=auto,onerror=redirect/uploads/asset/file/af423819-0aa0-4c89-8dc5-0e2db90d43a6/watch-the-loom.png?t=1787784657)](https://www.empanada.social/?utm_campaign=how-starface-made-pimple-patches-cool-the-complete-marketing-strategy&utm_medium=referral&utm_source=www.marketergems.com#video)

Your best hedge against rising LinkedIn CPMs: **organic reach**

But not how you think…

Instead of putting more ad dollars towards more expensive reach, activate your team by empowering them with organic posts.

I put together a 4-minute video showing exactly how Empanada does this.

If it looks like something your team could use, hit reply and I'll get you set up.

## What is Starface

> [![Image 3: Instagram post](https://beehiiv-images-production.s3.amazonaws.com/uploads/asset/file/6ace101c-e530-4c87-8490-401e2eb3f09f/instagram_screenshot_Clrvf14vjEg_1788971503_41fe9501.jpeg?t=1788971511)](https://www.marketergems.com/p/starface-marketing-strategy-deep-dive)

**Starface makes star-shaped hydrocolloid pimple patches**, the kind you slap on a breakout and wear proudly instead of hiding under makeup.

## Starface Target Demographics and Positioning

Starface hits a sweet spot that traditionally drove beauty marketers crazy: late Gen Z and early Gen Alpha consumers, roughly aged 13 to 24. They value **authenticity, humor, and self-acceptance over perfection**.

The brand’s positioning can be understood in 2 major parts:

### 1. Identity Over Utility

Teenagers don't want to be told their skin problem is invisible or fixable in three days.

They want permission to **not be perfect and still feel cool**.

Instead of designing patches to blend in, Starface made them bright, star-shaped, and impossible to miss - flipping the usual hide-your-blemish narrative into something closer to a fashion statement, built around empowerment rather than shame.

People often don't buy wearables for the function; they buy what wearing it signals to everyone else.

### 2. High-Visibility Visual Ownership

In marketing, if your product usage is invisible, you have to pay for every single impression through ads. But **if your product usage is hyper-visible, your customers pay you to become walking billboards**.

Starface claimed ownership of bright colours on human faces, which serves as an un-skippable, zero-CAC advertisement.

### 1. Product Design as Primary Customer Acquisition

Most brands design a product and then figure out how to market it. Starface designed the product specifically so the marketing was inherent to its usage.

According to brand commentary on early product strategy, founder Julie Schott realized that hydrocolloid sheets bought in bulk from medical suppliers could be die-cut into any shape without losing their fluid-absorbing properties.

Choosing a yellow star was deliberate:

*   The **yellow stars remind people of the reward stickers** kids get for doing well, turning acne into something positive.

*   The **bright yellow feels playful and cheerful**, making acne feel less serious or embarrassing.

*   Instead of hiding acne, the bright stars make it visible and**encourage people to talk about it** openly.

*   The yellow stars are instantly recognizable and give the brand a visual identity that **stands out online** and on shelves.

Because the product looks fun, users naturally want to share it. The product design systematically solves the top-of-funnel customer acquisition challenge.

### 2. TikTok-Native Unfiltered Organic Content

Starface was in favor of hyper-casual, creator-led TikTok content.

> [![Image 4: Instagram post](https://beehiiv-images-production.s3.amazonaws.com/uploads/asset/file/c9179118-c7ed-42c2-8fac-31821f62127a/instagram_screenshot_DXrtW2CD9Eg_1788971462_c937badd.jpeg?t=1788971470)](https://www.marketergems.com/p/starface-marketing-strategy-deep-dive)

Their content strategy relies on three main pillars:

*   **Casual Normalization:** Creators filming routine vlogs while casually wearing Starface patches without addressing them directly. This embeds the product into everyday life as normal attire.

*   **Character Personification:** Giving "Big Yellow" (their mascot case) a voice and **personality across social channels**. The brand speaks like a peer in comment sections, using current internet slang, participating in trending audio formats, and self-referential humor rather than corporate PR speak.

![Image 5](https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,quality=80,format=auto,onerror=redirect/uploads/asset/file/c2d8bb6b-a101-42b9-8246-38657975ab16/image.png?t=1788971361)

*   **UGC Amplification:** Aggressively reposting real customer videos showing the satisfaction of peeling off the patch after it absorbs fluid. It captures the **gross-yet-satisfying fascination** that drives massive engagement on short-form video platforms.

> [![Image 6: Instagram post](https://beehiiv-images-production.s3.amazonaws.com/uploads/asset/file/54c6a505-71d3-4a44-a81d-889fdedb0294/instagram_screenshot_C_kMtZxRBOl_1788971433_2a4781f4.jpeg?t=1788971438)](https://www.marketergems.com/p/starface-marketing-strategy-deep-dive)

### 3. IP Collaborations and Limited-Edition Collectibility

To prevent brand fatigue around the basic yellow star, Starface built a **streetwear-inspired drop model using brand partnerships**. They brought the hype-beast playbook to skincare.

They partnered with iconic cultural IPs including Sanrio (Hello Kitty, Kuromi, Keroppi), SpongeBob SquarePants, and Sesame Street.

> [![Image 7: Instagram post](https://beehiiv-images-production.s3.amazonaws.com/uploads/asset/file/640bab68-bed8-4de7-a954-3079fcdeb9fe/instagram_screenshot_DFqlIp6z9wy_1788971416_b399a303.jpeg?t=1788971422)](https://www.marketergems.com/p/starface-marketing-strategy-deep-dive)

These collaborations serve two strategic purposes:

*   **Re-engagement Hooks:** Existing customers who already own the standard yellow stars repurchase the new drop simply to collect the custom compacts and limited-edition patch designs.

*   **Audience Crossover:** Tapping into nostalgia-driven fandoms expands their reach into older Gen Z and Millennial audiences who grew up with these characters.

### 4. Retail Expansion: From DTC Darlings to Everyday Accessibility

While DTC built the brand's cultural relevance, retail drove scale.

Starface systematically expanded into physical retail channels where their core demographic shops daily: Target, Walmart, Sephora, and Ulta.

> [![Image 8: Instagram post](https://beehiiv-images-production.s3.amazonaws.com/uploads/asset/file/b6c009db-9b9c-4e5c-aa06-a031bd220989/instagram_screenshot_DNBCCv6RtXG_1788971397_f7d3c06f.jpeg?t=1788971404)](https://www.marketergems.com/p/starface-marketing-strategy-deep-dive)

In physical retail environments dominated by clinical whites, blues, and pale pastels, **Starface stands out visually**, capturing impulse buys at checkout from shoppers who saw the product online.

## The Rise of Wearables in Skincare

[WGSN](https://www.wgsn.com/en/blog/key-takeaways-cosmoprof-bologna-worldwide-2025?utm_campaign=how-starface-made-pimple-patches-cool-the-complete-marketing-strategy&utm_medium=referral&utm_source=www.marketergems.com) predicts that “fun-tility” (fun + utility) products are on the rise.

Starface helped kickstart a broader industry transition toward **functional skincare wearables**.

For years, skincare was invisible - creams absorb, serums disappear, and clear treatments blend in. But today, consumers actively seek out skincare products that display immediate, visual proof of use.

We see this across several emerging categories:

*   **Under-Eye Patches as Fashion:** Brands like Dieux Skin made reusable silicone eye masks an aesthetic statement, with users wearing them on flights, in coffee shops, and during morning routines on camera.

*   **LED Light Therapy Masks:** Devices like the Dennis Gross Spectralite or Omnilux turned high-tech treatments into futuristic, wearable status symbols shared across Instagram and TikTok.

*   **Somatic and Micro-Dart Patches:** Pimple patch technology expanded into targeted micro-dart delivery systems for deep cystic spots, dark spots, and wrinkles, making localized skin treatment visible and tactile.

Starface proved that **consumers are willing to wear their treatments publicly if the design grants them social currency**. Skincare moved from a private bathroom activity to a public lifestyle performance.

## Campaigns Starface Could Run Next

### 1. The Night Shift

A campaign focusing on the link between stress, late-night studying/working, and cortisol-induced breakouts.

Starface introduces an expanded overnight recovery line paired with calming, night-routine content.

### 2. Starface x Athletics

Breakouts among student-athletes and gym-goers are common due to sweat, friction, and gear.

This campaign positions Starface as essential athletic gear. In the locker room, in the gym bag, on the traveling bus, etc. Lace up your sneakers, slip on your jersey, and of course, stick on a Starface patch.

## Wrap Up

Starface proves that you don't always need to reinvent the underlying science to disrupt a multi-billion dollar category. Sometimes, you just need to change the narrative frame.

They understood a fundamental truth about modern marketing: **when your product turns your customer into a self-expressive advocate, your growth engine runs on real identity, not just ad spend**.

As skincare continues to evolve toward **functional wearables**, the brands that win will design experiences that consumers are proud to wear in public.

✌️,

Tom from Marketer Gems

kept.heading: AI, TOOLS AND TRANSFORMATION (8 MINUTE READ)
kept.blurb: AI will not eliminate software so much as change how companies decide what gets automated, standardized, or left improvised. Most employees do not naturally identify the workflows that should become software, and important processes often span multiple teams and systems, so successful automation still requires people who can spot problems, design solutions, and get the organization to adopt them. AI will expand existing software and make tools like spreadsheets, email, and chatbots more capable, while also creating new vertical applications that move work between improvised and institutionalized systems. The bigger opportunity for businesses is to look beyond faster versions of existing workflows and identify new products, services, and operating models that AI makes possible for the first time.

Title: AI, tools and transformation — Benedict Evans

URL Source: https://www.ben-evans.com/benedictevans/2026/9/3/ai-tools-and-transformation

Published Time: 2026-09-03T21:26:04+0000

Markdown Content:
AI, tools and transformation
It’s very tempting to imagine that AI turns everyone into a tool-builder - now everyone can just ask the model to make the software they need, and apps as we know them are dead. I think that misunderstands how most people think and where software actually comes from, and more importantly, it isn’t a path to change how companies actually work.

The typical big American company today has hundreds, and perhaps thousands, of different pieces of software. It has giant ‘big iron’ horizontal systems of record like SAP and Workday, it has hundreds of vertical SaaS applications, and then there are hundreds more workflows, scripts, automations and databases, right down to the 10 meg spreadsheet running a department. Very often, the company doesn’t even know quite how much it has, what’s actually being used, and what it’s paying for. And yet, with all this software, the company is full of boring, repetitive tasks.

It can be very tempting to think that AI will sweep most of this away. There’s an old joke that an engineer is someone who’ll spend an hour building a tool to automate a task that would take 10 minutes. But with AI, now you can make that tool in five minutes, and you don't need to be an engineer, and you don’t need to write code. You can just ask the model to make the tool for you, or, more fundamentally, _just do the task for you itself_. Instead of having to create those tools one at a time, software might be dynamic, generative, free-form, and spontaneous. Massively more tasks can be automated, with massively less software.

If you’re a tool-builder, and everybody in Silicon Valley is a tool-builder, this is intoxicating. But I think it misunderstands where software comes from and how people use it, and I think it misses how companies change.

First of all, most people are not tool builders, and most people don’t instinctively think about how their job could be done in a different way. If you spend all your time in the Silicon Valley bubble, it can be easy to forget this, because your entire world is about creating tools that change how things are done. But if you’re a really great matrimonial lawyer, you spend all your day thinking about your cases and your clients, not about what great legal discovery software would do; if you’re a really great enterprise salesperson, you spend all your time thinking about your product and your clients and your competitors, not about how great sales enablement software could make you more productive.

Products like Excel try to bridge this problem with on-boarding flows, assistants, and templates - everything you see in ‘File/New’ is a suggestion for what you could do with this. But every one of those templates still became a company, and that’s what I see in things like Claude for X as well - this is helpful, but not the answer.

Narrowly, that means that the task to be automated might be sitting in plain sight but the people with that task don’t see it. This is what leads to the idea of the ‘forward-deployed engineer’ - someone who _is_ a builder, and knows what AI can build, can ‘just’ walk around a law firm or an architecture office and see the opportunities lying on the table that the lawyer or the architect doesn't see. (This is also the experience of a lot of people in tech when they were 15, wandering around an internship or their parents’s office - “um, daddy, did you realise you could just do it like this?”).

The deeper problem is most of what we’ve automated in the last few decades wasn’t obvious, even if you are a tool-builder, and didn’t have an obvious solution either. We can all think of examples of stuff we use every day where our first reaction was “Why would I want that?” Very often, it's not obvious that the problem exists, and very often it's embedded or bundled or hidden inside something else. Equally, even if you can see the problem, or think you can, the right way to fix it often isn’t clear either, and the way to fix it is to redefine it or unbundle it, and working that out is hard. For many successful software companies, there were half a dozen failed attempts that came before and didn't find quite the right approach or the right problem.

None of this is solved by making easier to write code - by making it easier to make tools. The hard part is knowing that you need a tool for this in the first place, and then knowing what the tool should do.

But even once you reach that point, you have to get everybody else to use it, too. Many of the problems, workflows and tasks that we might want to automate touch 50 or 500 people across five different departments, three different systems of record, and four different regulatory regimes. You might have a great idea for doing an accounts payable differently, but you yourself can't change how everybody in the company does it. That has to be a purchase, and a decision, and an 18-month sales process.

Second, all of this means that software is bought or chosen or created on a spectrum from top-down to bottom-up - the company buys SAP and the user makes a spreadsheet - and I think it’s useful to think of this also as a spectrum from institutionalised to improvised.

You have tasks that are easy to do in the dedicated tools you already have, whether it’s SAP, Carta or Rippling. These tasks and workflows have been institutionalized - a bunch of people in those companies and your company have spent a lot of time working out the correct way to do that task, and it’s important that everyone do it the same way with the same tools. But then you have edge cases, exceptions and one-off questions, that are hard or impossible to do in those tools. Your users, bottom-up and creating their own solutions, manage these in a fuzzy, improvised space of freeform substrates like Excel, email, shared folders, Tableau, Powerpoint and CSVs, screenshots, PDFs and conference calls.

But once this task becomes something that you're doing all the time, in the same way every time, and that lots of people are doing, and becomes important and has revenue and risk attached to it, then, at a certain point, the company has to institutionalize it. You need audit, security, maintenance and accountability. You pave the [desire path](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desire_path) and pay someone to set it in stone. As above, you might not realize that the path is there - you might not realise that you have hundreds of people wasting an hour a day doing this - and it might be hard to work out the right way to fix that, but that process is why the company has hundreds of apps.

We went though a lot of this with the shift to SaaS, which was another order-of-magnitude change in how much software we had, along with a new operating model and a new cycle time, and that killed a lot of incumbents that couldn’t make the jump (the real rationale for the ‘SaaSpocalypse’). It’s a continuous and organic flow of bundling and unbundling. All of those SaaS apps do something that you _could_ do in SAP or Excel or email - Carta is a $4bn company that manages one spreadsheet for your CFO - and sometimes tasks move back. A few years ago I spoke to a consultant who said that half of their jobs were telling people who used Excel to use a database and the other half were the other way around.

Hence, if you’re PwC and you hire 3-4,000 graduates every year, you use dedicated, ‘institutionalised’ software to manage that. If you’re a small firm and you hire five or ten, you use email, a shared folder and Google Sheets. As that small firm grows, at a certain point it will outgrow that, and maybe move to Notion, or to an SME-focused SaaS HCM. But a small team inside PwC might also be using Google Sheets to track candidates to fill a role because Workday is too inflexible - the unbundling begins again.

Now AI rolls across all that. AI will expand all of the existing apps, and there’ll be many new vertical apps, and Excel, and Tableau, Google Sheets, email and all the other freeform spaces for improvising solutions will gain new capabilities. With that cycle, the chatbot itself is a new freeform space that sits next to Excel and email, taking over tasks from them and from your apps, and also losing tasks to those apps.

Now that small company hiring ten graduates might stick in Google sheets a lot longer because AI makes it more scalable, or you might use it as a data store for Gemini, and you might ask “should we get Claude to make something or move this to Notion?”… and then you see there’s a new SaaS app aimed right at you that solves this plus some other problem you haven’t thought of. AI doesn’t change the question: it creates new choices and moves the thresholds.

I think you can see all of this in the experience of enterprise AI deployment in the last three years. Every big company gave everyone Copilot (or maybe ChatGPT or Claude) and a small number of people are using this a lot (some of whom actually increased their productivity), while a larger set of people are using it a couple of times a week and a lot of the rest of your company isn't really using it at all. This is partly a change management and a training problem, but it's mostly the same problem that you would have had if you'd given everyone in the company a PC and Lotus 123 in 1983, or an internet connection and a web browser in 1997. How exactly does this map to everybody's tasks and the problems they actually have this week? Yes, you did give everybody a PC and Lotus, but that wasn’t how you transformed the efficiency of your invoice processing. Yes, you gave everybody a web browser, but that wasn't how you rebuilt your supply chain management around the internet, and it certainly wasn't how a retailer managed e-commerce.

Narrowly, the way that companies think about changing those kinds of structural processes is to start doing pilots. You run trials of products (both bought and built internal)that use the new capabilities of AI to automate processes that you couldn't automate before. There’s now all sorts of data around how many of these pilots there are, how many work (roughly half, as is normal - this is why they’re _pilots_!) and what can go wrong.

But again, this is a very old-fashioned CIO conversation around use cases, lighthouses, pilots, heroes, quick wins and measurable results. Meanwhile, the CEO and the board scratch their heads and say “Wait, but we've got 100s of workflows and we've done five or 10 pilots. That doesn’t seem to scale?” Giving everyone in the company ChatGPT does scale theoretically, except that most people aren't really finding ways to use it.

Going back to a hypothetical bank giving everyone spreadsheets in the 1980s, or a retailer giving everyone a web browser in the 1990s, yes, of course you should do that, and yes, of course, you need to think about training and change management and all the other good stuff that KPMG can tell you about. But that isn’t how you think about transforming the way your company works around a generational new technology.

Stepping back, it seems to me that with each new transformative technology, every company has to ask three kinds of questions. First, how do we buy, build and deploy this? Do we do pilots? Should we take the product that's bundled from Microsoft/Google/Oracle, build something ourselves, pay someone to build something, or buy this new thing from a startup? Second, they have to ask how far this changes their operations. What does it mean? What does email mean for us? What does spreadsheets mean for us? The answer to that might be radically different if you were an insurance company or a law firm. And third, you have to ask whether this creates new challenges to your business’s economics, new competitive pressures, or, perhaps, some kind of existential threat.

You don’t answer those questions by giving everyone Claude for X. Indeed, all of this means lots of new pitches for professional services (which is ironical given how many questions AI poses to their own business models). Do you want to work out how to deploy an LLM-enabled voice analytics tool in your call center? You're probably going to call Accenture. The vendors themselves have always been happy to help, and now the big labs have their own ‘deploycos’ - we used to joke that a ‘machine learning scientist’ is a statistician who lives in San Francisco, so maybe a ‘forward deployed engineer’ is anyone that OpenAI hired from a systems integrator. On the other side, your startup is building a great new tool and you want to go to market quickly? You'll probably call the Big Four. You're frustrated with how hard it is to sell AI software into law firms or accountancy firms. Okay - go start an ‘AI-enabled’ law firm and work out if that can be a key point of leverage (or whether it's like starting a ‘PC-enabled law firm’ in the 1980s). And of course, if you’re the board, and you're trying to work out whether this is some kind of existential threat or a massive revenue opportunity, then you’ll think about calling Bain, BCG and McKinsey (or your friendly neighborhood M&A banker) - this is what they do.

Stepping back from all of this, though, there's also a much simpler way to think about the question. With every new technology, we start by using it for the work we already have, and we just do that more and faster. But then, over time, you make entirely new things. We will use AI to automate broad classes of stuff inside existing workflows and existing companies (although, as I’ve outlined above, that will be enormously more trouble and work than just giving everybody a model). But with every previous platform shift, the stuff that actually mattered was the stuff that wasn't even possible before and that no-one even imagined.

Since it was launched nearly 36 years ago, [IMDb](https://variety.com/t/imdb/) has served as an online directory of TV shows and movies and the actors who appear in them.

Now Amazon-owned IMDb is adding “Digital Creator” as a new professional category on both IMDb and IMDbPro.

Digital creators who work in film, TV, streaming and branded entertainment already have listings on the service, like [MrBeast](https://www.imdb.com/name/nm10055663/) (Jimmy Donaldson), the most-followed individual YouTube creator whose projects have included reality series “Beast Games” for Prime Video.
