The “Digital Creator” designation functions as a professional category on IMDb and IMDbPro. Creators can feature multiple professions on their page, so someone who is both a digital creator and an actor can “represent the full scope of their work in one place,” per the company. No existing film or TV credits are required to establish a profile as a Digital Creator. The “Digital Creator” option is now available as a professional category for IMDbPro Premium members.

“IMDbPro empowers entertainment professionals with tools that help them get discovered, build their reputation, and advance their careers,” said Nikki Santoro, CEO of IMDb, in a statement. “Digital creators and their representatives need that same infrastructure, and producers, casting directors, studio executives and brand partners need a reliable way to find them. We’re excited to add a category that bridges that gap and gives creators a discoverable industry profile.”

IMDb’s launch of Digital Creator profiles will be “celebrated” at the Toronto International Film Festival where IMDb will host an invite-only industry cocktail party on Sept. 14. The TIFF event will mark the debut of the Digital Creator professional category and “spotlight IMDb’s expanding collaboration with Canadian guilds,” the company said.

IMDb said it will continue to expand professional categories based on industry feedback.

Key Points

*   Washington announced it would ban imports of Canadian motorbikes as well as many dairy and alcohol products from Sept. 29. 
*   Canada on Tuesday brought what it called “dollar for dollar” retaliatory tariffs on 27.6 billion Canadian dollars ($20 billion) of U.S. imports, targeting hundreds of products including furniture, household appliances, beauty products, clothing, agricultural equipment and more. 
*   Tensions between the countries continue to mount, with representatives from both sides accusing the other of discriminatory practices and saying they are standing up for domestic workers.

The White House said it would ban imports of Canadian motorbikes and a slew of other products starting later this month as diplomatic and trade relations with Ottawa continue to fray.

U.S. President [Donald Trump](https://www.cnbc.com/donald-trump/) on Tuesday signed executive orders to announce bans on Canadian whey products and molasses, nonalcoholic beer and a slew of alcoholic drinks including malt beer, wines, cider, whiskies, vodka and other spirits. Larger-capacity motorcycles and mopeds will also be banned.

The import restrictions, which largely replace tariffs of 50%, are due to take effect on Sept. 29, 2026.

![Image 12: Kelly Ann Shaw: This is a trade row rather than a full blown trade war](https://image.cnbcfm.com/api/v1/image/108359653-3ED1-MC-090826-Kelly.jpg?v=1788864321&w=750&h=422&vtcrop=y)

The U.S. also [announced](https://www.whitehouse.gov/fact-sheets/2026/09/fact-sheet-president-donald-j-trump-responds-to-canadas-retaliation/?) that tariffs on other Canadian products would be modified and extended from Sept. 15, including the addition of all-terrain vehicles and animal hides, and the removal of rock salt and cement.

U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said the moves were a “natural consequence of Canada’s continued discriminatory treatment of crucial American exports.”

It was announced on the same day that [Canadian tariffs on 27.6 billion Canadian dollars ($20 billion) of U.S. imports](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/09/08/canada-retaliatory-tariffs.html) came into effect, targeting more than 700 goods across steel, dairy, farm equipment, pulp and paper, electronics, and more.

Those “dollar for dollar” tariffs were issued in retaliation for the [50% duties the U.S. slapped on Canadian](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/07/20/trump-tariffs-canada-trade.html) hockey sticks, wine and a range of other goods over Ottawa’s alleged trade discrimination. The U.S. tariffs took effect Aug. 22, hours after trade talks between the two countries fell apart.

The two sides have [continued to blame one another](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/09/03/carney-lutnick-trump-trade-canada.html) for the failure to reach a deal, and accused the other of unfair practices that harm their domestic workers.

Trump has accused Canada of disadvantaging U.S. exports through its policies in the auto, alcohol and dairy sectors, highlighting the [U.S.′ trade deficit in goods](https://ustr.gov/countries-regions/americas/canada), and [threatening to hit cars, trucks and auto parts](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/08/24/trump-canada-auto-tariffs-trade-war.html) with a 50% tariff from Jan. 1, 2027.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said in an August address that the “narrow merchandise trade deficit only exists because the U.S. buys so much of its energy from us,” and flagged that Canada is the biggest consumer for U.S. cars and steel.

On Tuesday, Carney said Canada’s tariffs would “come with a cost” but were necessary to protect businesses, workers and communities.

The existing tariffs apply to a relatively small portion of the $715.5 billion trade in goods between the countries, but [economists have warned](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/08/24/canada-us-trade-war-deal.html) of an immediate blow to small- and medium-sized businesses and of the risks to growth from further escalation.

“Companies on both sides of the border will need to wait to see if these tariffs hold, more measures are enacted, or each country decides to de-escalate. In the meantime, those businesses will realize both tariff-, compliance-, and uncertainty-related costs,” said Justin Angotti, associate in the international trade and national security group at law firm Reed Smith.

Ottawa is meanwhile eyeing closer trade and security ties with the European Union as its relationship with Washington deteriorates, [Bloomberg reported Tuesday.](https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-09-08/eu-and-canada-plan-far-reaching-alliance-to-strengthen-partnership)

## [](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/09/09/us-canada-trade-war-import-ban.html)Alcohol wars

Beer and spirits sales have emerged as a political flashpoint as relations between the U.S. and Canada have deteriorated.

Stores in several Canadian provinces have removed U.S. alcohol from their shelves, public campaigns have called for boycotts and Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe in August announced a 50% tariff on American ‌imports.

Moe’s team told CNBC this week that the alcohol levy was a “reciprocal measure” intended to support local businesses and encourage progress toward a fair and balanced trade resolution.

U.S. spirits exports to Canada fell more than 70% year on year from the start of the retaliatory ban in March 2025 through December 2025, according to the Distilled Spirits Council of the United States.

Chris Swonger, president and CEO of the trade association, said American distillers had “shouldered the brunt of this trade dispute.”

“We appreciate President Trump’s recognition of the significant harm these sales bans have caused U.S. distillers and urge leaders on both sides of the border to reach a negotiated solution that restores U.S. spirits to retail shelves throughout Canada and returns the spirits sector to a permanent zero-for-zero tariff framework,” Swonger said.

Title: 2026 Google Ranking Factors Expert Survey

URL Source: https://signal.zyppy.com/p/google-ranking-factors-expert-survey

Published Time: 2026-09-09T13:08:41+00:00

Markdown Content:
_👋 Subscribe free (it helps us produce research like this) and get tips + tactics on how to win more SEO and AI visibility._

We asked **131 SEOs**, including [some of the most respected in the industry](https://signal.zyppy.com/i/214631214/contributors-google-ranking-factors-expert-survey-2026), _what factors are most important for ranking on Google in 2026_.

And they delivered.

Lots has changed in SEO since [Rand Fishkin published the very first Ranking Factor survey in 2005](https://web.archive.org/web/20070406043151/http://www.seomoz.org/article/search-ranking-factors-2005). Since then, we've had the **emergence of AI**, revelations from **API leaks and antitrust trials**, and multiple **Google algorithm changes**. To keep up, _we designed this survey to reflect these newer factors, and we're honored to carry on the tradition._

In total, our experts generously contributed **13,665 ranking-factor data points** for analysis. To our knowledge, this is one of the largest and most up-to-date collections of external expert knowledge on how Google actually works.

## How We Measured Ranking Factors

*   Each expert scored and evaluated more than **100 potential Google ranking factors**. Respondents were asked, “_How much of a positive or negative effect do you believe each of the following factors has on Google’s organic search rankings?_“

*   Respondents then rated each factor on a **7-point scale,**from +3 (Strongly Positive) to -3 (Strongly Negative).

*   Finally, the respondents were asked an **open-ended question**: “_What are the three most important Google_ _ranking factors?_“ For this question, they could answer anything they wanted.

After crunching the numbers, while the most critical ranking factors haven’t changed tremendously from past years, the details matter - _especially in terms of AI, user click signals, and deeper content characteristics_.
According to our experts, the most important Google ranking signals in 2026 are

**Relevance**, **Backlinks**, and **Content Quality.**We’ve listed the top 10 below, along with the percentage (%) of respondents who selected it as a “top 3” factor.

**1. Relevance - 57.1%:**Content is relevant if it _matches and satisfies the search intent of the user_. The content should semantically match what the user is looking for and satisfy their needs.

**2. Backlinks - 54.8%:**The rumor of the death of backlinks has been greatly exaggerated. In fact, respondents rated links from trusted, relevant sites as one of the most important factors. Many experts emphasize the importance of links from pages with real visitors.

**3. Content Quality - 47.6%:**Nearly half of our experts listed elements of content quality as a top-ranking factor. This includes features such as originality, accuracy, and freshness.

**4. Authority & Trust - 36.5%:**How much Google trusts the website, creator, or brand/business.

**5. Behavior / Click Signals - 29.4%:**How users select search results and interact with web pages. Google watches the user.

**6. Brand Signals - 27.0%:**The importance of being a brand/entity that people search for, trust, and visit.

**7. User Satisfaction - 19.8%**: User satisfaction or “task completion” as the ultimate outcome.

**8. Technical SEO Health - 17.5%**: Crawling and indexing form the foundation for all other ranking factors.

**9. Topical Authority - 14.3%:**How well your brand/site is associated with expertise on a particular topic.

**10. Internal Links - 11.1%:**How you connect web pages on your site through links and site architecture.

Let’s dig deeper into the individual factors to see what matters. You can find **definitions** for many of the [ranking factors here](https://zyppy.com/ranking-factor-definitions/).

Out of all the over 100 ranking factors we quizzed our experts on, “**Search Intent Match**“ was the clear winner.

Search Intent Match is defined as _“How well the page satisfies the type of result or task the searcher appears to want.”_ Notably, this goes beyond simply matching keywords and semantic relevance, because our experts say you actually need to give users what they want.

Surprisingly (or not), the lowly **Meta Description** was rated so ineffective that most SEOs don’t believe it has any impact.

[![Image 1: Melissa Popp](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!ZM8v!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F0806f553-c3e6-4a13-9d0e-4a2bde64f95a_1201x87.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!ZM8v!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F0806f553-c3e6-4a13-9d0e-4a2bde64f95a_1201x87.png)

_**“**You can have technically perfect content with pristine headings and a gorgeous URL structure, but if the person searching wanted one thing and you answered another, **none of that saves you**.**”**_

[![Image 2: Andy Chadwick](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!O2I8!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F3b408103-8ed3-4416-9ebd-c8b8c8c2deae_1201x87.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!O2I8!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F3b408103-8ed3-4416-9ebd-c8b8c8c2deae_1201x87.png)

_**“**I’d add **information gain**. Once ten pages all match the intent and cover the same ground, what decides it is whether a page adds something the others don’t.**”**_

[![Image 3: Shai Aharony](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!8F5R!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F2856590f-94bd-43e5-8eaf-814410606423_1201x87.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!8F5R!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F2856590f-94bd-43e5-8eaf-814410606423_1201x87.png)

_**“**I’m just as surprised as everyone else by **how effective EMDs are still**. We are ranking an EMD for a competitive term with a fraction of the effort for our main site that is competing for the same term.**”**_

Who says you don’t need backlinks anymore?

“**Links from highly trusted domains**” and from “**topically relevant pages**” were two of the highest-rated factors across the entire survey.

Meanwhile, even though Google says they ignore most spam links, these were rated as one of the biggest negative ranking factors.

[![Image 4](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!IixX!,w_2400,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fdcaed2f0-c261-41b4-a0bd-283978135e69_1201x1090.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!IixX!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fdcaed2f0-c261-41b4-a0bd-283978135e69_1201x1090.png)

[![Image 5: Nitin Manchanda](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!A8Nd!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F938bdb75-860f-4cd6-936c-bb0bd86744a2_1201x87.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!A8Nd!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F938bdb75-860f-4cd6-936c-bb0bd86744a2_1201x87.png)

_**“**A hundred links from **real audiences** beat a thousand links nobody ever clicks.**”**_

[![Image 6: Andrew Shotland](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!hUf4!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fdf2239ee-7b98-4d49-9a05-d6a03277b11b_1201x87.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!hUf4!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fdf2239ee-7b98-4d49-9a05-d6a03277b11b_1201x87.png)

_**“**With AI, links can have an even greater effect. A client recently got mentioned and linked from a Reuters article a few weeks ago. Their visibility in ChatGPT went up **4x over the next week**.**”**_

[![Image 7: Geoff Kenyon](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!gUax!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F764f7024-d54b-46ca-8ca7-0aaff9e3ae01_1201x87.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!gUax!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F764f7024-d54b-46ca-8ca7-0aaff9e3ae01_1201x87.png)

_**“**Exact match anchors cut both ways. They drive real gains up to a point and suppress performance past it. The variable is what **share of the anchor profile they represent**, not the raw count.**”**_

Content Quality is where our ranking factors begin to diverge significantly from past surveys.

“**Original Research**” and “**First-Party Data**” top the list, reflecting the importance of producing unique, non-commodity content in the age of AI.

**Many saw AI-generated content**negatively, but only when it is _scaled with little added value_.

> “Using AI to help you publish ten times the amount of the same quality content in half the time is not as good as using AI to help you publish the same amount of content, _but ten times the quality_.”
> 
> 
> - [Everett Sizemore](https://esizemore.com/)

[![Image 8](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!wo3x!,w_2400,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fe1ea384f-8412-4f0e-aab8-5cff3c76a152_1201x1588.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!wo3x!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fe1ea384f-8412-4f0e-aab8-5cff3c76a152_1201x1588.png)

[![Image 9: Gianluca Fiorelli](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!8Rkr!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fa19d0095-0a16-425e-b7c5-510230a8dc70_1201x87.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!8Rkr!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fa19d0095-0a16-425e-b7c5-510230a8dc70_1201x87.png)

_**“**Too much consensus, and you’re invisible for not being relevant enough. Too much information gain, and you’re shadowbanned for being **too contrarian**.**”**_

[![Image 10: Ross Simmonds](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!mK7T!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fde4bc2cd-cc1b-4811-b68e-4df7b7e6a222_1201x87.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!mK7T!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fde4bc2cd-cc1b-4811-b68e-4df7b7e6a222_1201x87.png)

_**“**AI has made content cheap. Anyone can spin up a thousand articles overnight. And Google knows it. That’s why **quality is becoming the filter**. When the volume of content explodes, the cost of publishing drops to zero... but the cost of trust goes up.**”**_

[![Image 11: Abby Gleason](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!ZIik!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F7d993b6c-f91e-4f4b-b36e-6e8f85d7a327_1201x87.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!ZIik!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F7d993b6c-f91e-4f4b-b36e-6e8f85d7a327_1201x87.png)

_**“**I have seen positive results from **high-quality AI generation at scale**. This is on a site that has plenty of unique content and UGC, and AI content undergoes intensive human editor review.**”**_

Brand is one of the primary ways Google learns who to trust.

“**Online Reputation/Trust**” and “**Branded Search Volume**” (e.g., how many people search for you by name) were ranked as two of the most important factors.

An oldie-but-goodie, “Google Ad Spend,” snuck by with a barely positive influence, presumably because it can boost your visibility.

[![Image 12](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!2iw2!,w_2400,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fe949b710-b1db-4d25-a48c-b828af77e60b_1201x1077.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!2iw2!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fe949b710-b1db-4d25-a48c-b828af77e60b_1201x1077.png)

[![Image 13: Dan Petrovic, Dejan](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Jhj5!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F7e0e18a1-1a53-47ac-8a19-af62a955f180_1201x87.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Jhj5!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F7e0e18a1-1a53-47ac-8a19-af62a955f180_1201x87.png)

_**“**It's a **popularity contest**. Once Google finds you relevant for a query, it doesn't really reward 10x content... In fact, I'll go as far as to say that content that is too expert-level is actually harmful to visibility. You need to hit the Goldilocks zone where you appeal broadly to as many people as possible and get talked about, shared, linked, and mentioned.**”**_

[![Image 14: Jan-Willem Bobbink](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!YieM!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F3c4238d9-8f93-400a-8f9b-8ebbab1efdfb_1201x87.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!YieM!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F3c4238d9-8f93-400a-8f9b-8ebbab1efdfb_1201x87.png)

_**“**Brand signals are the **strongest factor** in my opinion. You can get away with a website technically in a very bad shape, without having optimized content as long as people search and talk about the brand.**”**_

[![Image 15: Roger Montti](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!7f_2!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fd6822f36-238f-4036-802f-8dd6f1433532_1201x87.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!7f_2!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fd6822f36-238f-4036-802f-8dd6f1433532_1201x87.png)

_**“**Branded Search is the **new link,** since 2012, if a Google patent is to be believed.**”**_

[![Image 16: Will Critchlow](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!iqB2!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fe77b55d7-3485-4cb6-9c96-5306ac92f4c2_1201x87.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!iqB2!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fe77b55d7-3485-4cb6-9c96-5306ac92f4c2_1201x87.png)

_**“**No **direct** effect of ad spend - it can affect other signals, though, so it can result in benefit.**”**_

With evidence revealed from Google’s antitrust trial and API leak, user-based signals took a big leap in this year’s survey.

SEOs now better understand how closely Google watches what users do.

“**Satisfaction/Task Completion**” was rated highest among the user signals, while “Return to SERP” (the searcher returns to Google's results after visiting the page) was rated negatively.

[![Image 17](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!GjiI!,w_2400,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F24e8372e-ebf5-4302-aee6-885538a989f9_1201x754.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!GjiI!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F24e8372e-ebf5-4302-aee6-885538a989f9_1201x754.png)

[![Image 18: AJ Kohn](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!deRk!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F96c7ca0d-bf2b-481e-a5d3-28d6db9a8baa_1201x87.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!deRk!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F96c7ca0d-bf2b-481e-a5d3-28d6db9a8baa_1201x87.png)

_**“**Navboost is still a monster. As such, sites really should create a **satisfaction metric** (often by page type) to try to emulate satisfaction. Because there is a ranking ceiling when click signals are worse than other SERP competitors.**”**_

[![Image 19: Gerry White](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!rbo_!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fca607a5e-a126-41e7-ab13-d8fe25f8cf71_1201x87.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!rbo_!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fca607a5e-a126-41e7-ab13-d8fe25f8cf71_1201x87.png)

_**“**Bounce rate is a bad metric, but sites where users **pogo-stick to another result**, I believe that is a clear signal that Google is absolutely taking.**”**_

[![Image 20: Diego Ivo](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!lVIj!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fafc401d7-0ec4-464c-a232-d31fa0e0f94d_1201x87.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!lVIj!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fafc401d7-0ec4-464c-a232-d31fa0e0f94d_1201x87.png)

_**“**User signals are the **final verdict** of search engines. My question is: when most browsing becomes agentic, how will they measure them?**”**_

Google's ability to **crawl and index** your pages forms the basis of SEO. As such, solid technical foundations make all other ranking factors possible.

Most respondents described technical SEO as “table stakes.” While bad technical SEO can definitely hurt, you shouldn’t expect good technical SEO to elevate otherwise mediocre content.

[![Image 21](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!qsLA!,w_2400,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F72f1b622-6f2c-4e9c-aa7c-4ff6787dd6f1_1201x1150.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!qsLA!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F72f1b622-6f2c-4e9c-aa7c-4ff6787dd6f1_1201x1150.png)

[![Image 22: Marshall Simmonds](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!oCRW!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fa5248b22-cbee-4552-b9bc-054da52d981f_1201x87.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!oCRW!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fa5248b22-cbee-4552-b9bc-054da52d981f_1201x87.png)

_**“**Tech SEO is a **commodity** at this point. It won’t necessarily win the race, but it can absolutely lose it.**”**_

[![Image 23: Dana DiTomaso](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!-I21!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F9f072dab-9570-4dc2-aedb-c56dfa9bf879_1201x87.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!-I21!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F9f072dab-9570-4dc2-aedb-c56dfa9bf879_1201x87.png)

_**“**We were working with a client who accidentally set their canonicals pointing at pages that weren’t at all similar to the original content. Once that was fixed they saw an almost **immediate positive change** in their impressions and clicks -- I think it was around +60%.**”**_

Title: Deepfakes are wrecking influencers’ credibility, one fake ad at a time

URL Source: https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/sep/12/deepfakes-wrecking-influencers-credibility

Published Time: 2026-09-12T12:00:34.000Z

Markdown Content:
E arlier this year, Emily Schuman, the creator of the lifestyle blog Cupcakes and Cashmere, saw a photo of herself she didn’t recognize on [Instagram](https://www.theguardian.com/technology/instagram). In a sponsored ad, Schuman, who has more than 500,000 Instagram followers, is holding up a vial of GLP-1 drugs, advertising the telehealth company Gala. There was just one problem: Schuman had never heard of Gala and had nothing to do with the ad.

The ad was based on a digitally altered version of a selfie Schuman had taken in her car and posted on Instagram years earlier. Once her followers got wind, they flooded her inbox with questions about the sponsorship as it didn’t seem consistent with Schuman’s personal brand. Soon after, Schuman discovered this was just the beginning. There was also an Instagram post where an AI version of her with darker hair appears to apply foundation to promote a makeup brand called Meroda Cosmetics, and [TikTok](https://www.theguardian.com/technology/tiktok) posts with generated images of her promoting the blood testing company Superpower.

“It’s so violating,” she said. The videos and images look “just like me, but the upside down version”.

Neither Gala nor Meroda responded to requests for comment. Superpower CEO Max Marchione said the TikTok post wasn’t a real ad, but instead came from a scammer his company later reported. “Whilst scamming isn’t new, AI has made this much worse,” he said.

As generative AI makes it easier to create text, code and media, it has also supercharged the creation of deepfakes, the synthetic photos and videos that can be nearly indistinguishable from reality. Influencers are some of the easiest people to impersonate due to the sheer amount of videos and images AI can learn from. The vulnerability represents a new workplace threat: influencers aren’t just competing for brand deals with other creators, but also fighting to preserve the credibility of their own likeness – the very asset that generates their income.

“Their brand is their business,” said Alice Marwick, the director of research at the Data & Society Research Institute, who published a recent paper on the rise of AI impersonation scams. “If their brand takes a hit, so does everything in their business life.”

On social media, impersonation schemes run a large spectrum, from deepfaked Elon Musk promoting a fraudulent cryptocurrency, to brands quietly scraping an influencer’s image to manufacture ads. Global consumers may have lost as much as $3.7bn due to deepfake scams in 2026, according to [an investigation](https://go.skimresources.com/?id=114047X1771840&url=https%3A%2F%2Fsurfshark.com%2Fresearch%2Fchart%2Fdeepfake-fraud-origins&sref=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.theguardian.com%2Ftechnology%2F2026%2Fsep%2F12%2Fdeepfakes-wrecking-influencers-credibility&xcust=referrer%7Cnone%7CaccountId%7C114047X1771840%7CabTestParticipations%7Cgrowth-auxia-banner%3Avariant%2Cidentity-and-trust-consent-rr-banner-us%3Avariant-2) from the VPN-maker Surfshark’s research team. The investigation found that social media impersonations on social media accounted for about half of all losses.

## Easy targets for deepfakes

Celebrities and influencers are often the easiest to impersonate because they “have hundreds of hours of footage and thousands of pictures of them online. So you can feed that into a model and produce a fairly convincing deepfake,” said Marwick. Taylor Swift, Oprah Winfrey, Kim Kardashian, Gwyneth Paltrow and Tom Hanks have all been deepfaked by AI to promote various products online.

But big celebrities aren’t alone. On Instagram, beauty influencer Arielle Lorre was deepfaked to promote a skincare brand. Fashion creator Jessi Caparella discovered altered images of herself on Pinterest redirecting traffic to affiliate clothing links. And deepfaked videos of OnlyFans creator Elaina St James were used to trick fans into sending money to fraudulent accounts. While the financial impact of these impersonation schemes is hard to pinpoint, creators say that deepfakes dilute their value, cost them the trust of their followers, and can be time-consuming to fight: even when one deepfake post is reported and removed, another one pops up in its place.

With AI, “impersonation is much easier and much more convincing … [so] scams can be operated at a much larger scale,” said Marwick. “It’s often really believable. And with every new frontier model, they get better and better.”

One reason for the rise of deepfakes may be a growing use of AI-generated marketing content in general. AI-generated or “virtual” influencers accounted for $1.37bn, or about 4% of all brand spending in 2026, according to [research](https://www.digitalapplied.com/blog/influencer-marketing-statistics-2026-data-points) from marketing consultancy Digital Applied. Virtual influencers may not have the same authenticity as real people, but they are much cheaper, always available, and infinitely customizable, which makes them attractive for some brand campaigns.

While the ad industry has always blurred the line between real and fake with airbrushing, CGI and other digital editing tools, the rise of AI has allowed brands to generate content from nothing with minimal production costs. And for some brands, that means crossing the line into deepfakes.

Influencers are doing whatever they can to fight the issue. Molly Tranchin, a fashion influencer known as FashionVeggie with more than 500,000 followers on Instagram, recently filed a [lawsuit](https://www.bloomberglaw.com/public/desktop/document/TranchinvEBYIncDocketNo326cv05559NDCalJun092026CourtDocket?doc_id=X112A6OV78U9H7Q8LATMEK31FFP) against the underwear brand Eby. According to the lawsuit, Tranchin had a contract to create three marketing videos for Eby in exchange for a fee. Eby was entitled to one round of “reasonable edits” for Tranchin to revise. The lawsuit claims that instead of posting the videos Tranchin submitted – in which she posed “modestly covering her chest and breasts with her arms” – the brand instead posted a deepfake video of Tranchin in a different pose, “exposing her breasts and nipples through one of Eby’s sheer bras”.

Tranchin has since dropped the lawsuit over a lack of jurisdiction and plans to refile it in a different court, according to court documents filed last month.

Eby spokesperson Clara Spahr said the company couldn’t comment on the pending litigation but will address the claims through the legal process.

## The fight for their likeness

Tranchin, whose lawsuit is ongoing, has the benefit of knowing exactly who to hold accountable for the deepfakes. Other creators are not as lucky.

When Schuman discovered the deepfaked ads using her likeness, she and her manager immediately reported them to [Meta](https://www.theguardian.com/technology/meta). She said many of her followers, who brought these ads to her attention, also reported them. But it took weeks of badgering before Meta removed the GLP-1 ad. The makeup ad still remains in circulation on Instagram, despite many attempts from Schuman to get it taken down.

Both Meta and TikTok explicitly prohibit using artificial intelligence or digital manipulation to replicate a person’s identity. But the reality is that these platforms’ personalization algorithms may inadvertently grease the wheels for these schemes.

Meta, for example, allows advertisers to use hyper-targeted audience slicing, meaning bad actors can quietly launch fraudulent ads, create new accounts if one gets flagged, and scale their reach rapidly. In response to complaints about rampant scams on its platforms, Meta introduced [new tools](https://about.fb.com/news/2026/03/fighting-scammers-protecting-people-with-new-technology-and-partnerships/) this year, including stronger advertiser verification policies and an AI detection tool to prevent “celeb-bait”, or the impersonation of celebrities. But experts say these tools do not go far enough, and that the company lacks incentive to clean up its own ad ecosystem. Meta did not respond to multiple requests for comment.

“The reality is that platforms make a lot of money off scams,” Marwick said.

Meta made about $16bn from ads promoting scams or banned goods, accounting for about 10% of its revenue in 2024, according to a [2025 investigation](https://www.reuters.com/investigations/meta-is-earning-fortune-deluge-fraudulent-ads-documents-show-2025-11-06/) from Reuters. That investigation also quoted an internal presentation from Meta’s safety team, which estimated that its platforms were “involved in a third of all successful scams in the US”.

Not only do deepfakes hurt brand deals for individual influencers, but they also challenge the entire influencer marketing ecosystem. They disrupt the already delicate premise that a real person trusts a product or brand, and therefore their followers should do the same.

Schuman said she is deciding whether or not she needs to retain legal counsel to help her fight off the deepfakes as they keep popping up. Besides reporting the offending posts and threatening legal action, influencers don’t have much recourse.

“That’s money and time lost,” Schuman said about hiring a lawyer. But the alternative is a hit to her reputation. “So it’s a lose-lose from all ways of looking at it.”

Title: Your playbook for LinkedIn ads that work

URL Source: https://www.growthunhinged.com/p/linkedin-ad-playbook

Published Time: 2026-09-13T13:50:00.000Z

Markdown Content:
[![Image 1](https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,quality=80,format=auto,onerror=redirect/uploads/asset/file/e2395fe2-5c43-4f0b-ae16-8761219a85bf/Newsletter_placement_-_ploy_image_-_Sept_13.png?t=1788988573)](https://ploy.ai/?utm_source=linkedin&utm_medium=creator&utm_campaign=kyle_poyar&utm_content=v1_09_06_2026)
_Growth Unhinged is proudly supported by Ploy_

_It’s become a cliché that the first thing a marketing leader wants to do is change the website. Well, dear readers, I’ve been that cliché… more than once._

_And I’ve lived to regret it. The refreshed website looked good, but it didn’t move the rest of the funnel._

_That’s why I’m so bullish on_ _**[Ploy](https://ploy.ai/?utm\_source=linkedin&utm\_medium=creator&utm\_campaign=kyle\_poyar&utm\_content=v1\_09\_06\_2026)**_ _, the marketing platform that turns your website into an always-on growth engine. Think of it as an AI growth teammate that works around the clock: building ABM pages, launching campaign landing pages, de-anonymizing website visitors, and automating growth workflows._

👋_Hi, it’s Kyle and welcome to_[_Growth Unhinged_](https://www.growthunhinged.com/subscribe)_, my weekly newsletter exploring the hidden playbooks behind the fastest-growing startups._

_In this newsletter I try to cover a wide spectrum of GTM. But there’s been a glaring gap: paid acquisition. For B2B, this increasingly means LinkedIn advertising. While far from cheap, LinkedIn ads have reach and the potential for hyper-precise targeting (_ _[as I featured previously](https://www.growthunhinged.com/p/a-very-tactical-guide-to-abm)_ _)._

_**Up today: a playbook for LinkedIn ads**_ _from performance marketer_ _[Bogdan Liutic](https://www.linkedin.com/in/bgdn/)_ _. Bogdan runs_ _[CR8](https://cr8.eco/)_ _, a tech-forward LinkedIn ads agency, and has founded two 7-figure businesses built on performance marketing._

A senior B2B buyer takes six to eight [touches](https://www.rainsalestraining.com/sales-research/sales-prospecting-research) before they even consider booking a call with you.

That's why ads by themselves, directing to book a demo or call, are not enough. That's why cold outreach by itself is not enough. And content by itself is not enough.

What you want is a flow. My LinkedIn ad playbook took me 14 years in growth marketing to figure out, and I’ve compressed it to 10 minutes of your time. You’ll walk away with:

*   Clarity on how LinkedIn ads actually work, what works, and what doesn't

*   A map for your own LinkedIn ad campaign

*   How to drop cost per lead with very specific hacks

![Image 2](https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,quality=80,format=auto,onerror=redirect/uploads/asset/file/f896b392-9b5d-474e-8a06-11da088a6ff4/image.png?t=1788453723)

## We all know LinkedIn ads are expensive, right?

I had a call with this client, let’s call him Mark. He targets CHROs of companies with 100+ employees in regulated industries. He wants more deals.

I asked him the classic discovery question: “What you tried before?”

“Well… In the last 8 months I’ve spent $30k on Linkedin ads and got 2 leads a month. Maybe 12 leads total, and 8 or 9 of those were the wrong type of lead."

I am telling you this story to illustrate a simple message. If you don’t nail the fundamentals, no amount of tactics will save you. So, let’s do the fundamentals.

To understand when LinkedIn ads do work, I propose to do the Charlie Munger move: invert. Understand when they don't work.

**First: your average contract value (ACV)**or lifetime value (LTV) should be at least $10,000. Otherwise the math just doesn’t fit.

The cost per thousand impressions (CPM) on LinkedIn is $37.42 on average according to [Dreamdata](https://dreamdata.io/linkedin-ads-b2b-benchmarks), roughly 3-4x Meta's $10.01. Expensive impressions are fine when one deal pays for months of them; at sub-$10k LTV, it’s tough.

**Second: your total addressable market (TAM)** on the decision-maker level should be at least 10,000 people. People are not sitting on LinkedIn all the time (surprise!). You need critical mass for LinkedIn ads to work at any given moment. Less than that, do direct outreach, do events.

Third, the obvious one: your ICP should actually be on LinkedIn. Selling to construction crews, cold calling is probably better. Selling to HR leaders, to C-level folks, good bet.

There's a reason LinkedIn ads are so expensive: the senior decision-makers ARE there. (And measured correctly, it's actually a cheap channel. It has the lowest cost-per-company-influenced of any social network at $76.42, and the only one with positive return-on-ad-spend; same Dreamdata 2026 report.)

Want to do a self-check-up? Use this [live calculator](http://cr8.eco/math) and put in your LTV, close rate (what percentage of qualified sales conversations you actually close), show rate, and media budget.

The goal is the LTV:CAC ratio: 3+ is a green light, 2-3 is workable, below 2, walk away.

![Image 3](https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,quality=80,format=auto,onerror=redirect/uploads/asset/file/1d96dabc-d2d2-4104-8272-d7db923df9bb/image.png?t=1788453972)

Here’s an example:

*   The company has a $30k LTV, 22% close rate, and 75% show-up rate.

*   They spend $3,000 per month on LinkedIn ads.

*   They can expect ~45 leads per quarter at ~$200 cost-per-lead.

*   These leads convert to ~15 completed meetings and ~3 deals per quarter.

*   The CAC is ~$3k on media spend alone, translating to ~3:1 LTV:CAC all-in once fees and sales compensation are included.

*   **Verdict: LinkedIn ads are scalable.**

One nuance: the average B2B customer journey is now 272 days from first marketing touch to closed revenue, and 81% of it happens before the sales pipeline based on a Dreamdata [study](https://dreamdata.io/linkedin-ads-b2b-benchmarks) of 3.5 million journeys. This includes 88 touches, 10 stakeholders, and 4 channels.

The ads help get you the sales call. There’s plenty of sales work to close the deal.

[Video 3](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=A-VzsDv47g8)

The conventional idea of an ad campaign looks something like this: go to Campaign Manager, see what filters are available, run some ads to the website, and expect people to book a call.

Results are… meh. You stop the ads, move somewhere else.

We already covered why one touch doesn't progress anything. But the other problem is the audience itself. Several examples of filters inside LinkedIn Ads that look cool but are trash:

*   **Member groups:**You can target members of very specific groups, but more often than not it's nobody. Groups are kinda dead on LinkedIn, and people forget they joined them years ago.

*   **Company revenue:** It’s not accurate. Work on headcount instead, and even that is not fully reliable.

*   **Member skills:**You're relying on how fully people actually fill out their profiles. I wouldn't go there.

LinkedIn has a lot of important business information, and you should use it. But it doesn't have all of it, and more often than not it doesn't have the most important kind. This is what we call signals.

Signals answer the question: what behavior, directly or indirectly, proves a company is in the buying window or about to be? If ideal customer profile (ICP) definitions and filters answer the question who, signals answer the question when.

For collecting signals you need a data source. But what makes a good one? Five criteria are needed for it to be usable (you can find industry-specific examples [here](http://cr8.eco/signals)):

*   **Public:**you can actually access it, no login wall.

*   **Dated:**you can tell two-week-old from two-year-old.

*   **Structured:** it can become a row in a spreadsheet.

*   **Frequent:**it updates often enough to reuse next month.

*   **Causal:** it points at real money moving, a repeated job post means salary budget and recruiting spend, a rebranded banner means nothing.

To make it more concrete, consider an HR tech company. We noticed an ICP-fit company posts a new job for their first-ever People Operations hire across three job boards. “Workday implementation” is inside the job description. All of these are signals that the prospect is buying HR tech right now or about to, on top of the conventional targeting of industry, company size, geo, and role.

I recommend getting signal data with an agentic flow:

*   **Step 1:**Find the data source. In HR tech, for instance, that's job boards like Indeed. In SaaS it can be technology data providers like BuildWith. Another option is industry-agnostic databases like Apollo.

*   **Step 2:** Pull and store the data. Apify for scraping, Notion for keeping the information, Claude for reading it.

*   **Step 3:** Make it recurring. New companies enter the space every week so the list renews weekly in the best case.

No stack? No problem! Open your 30 target accounts' careers pages every Friday, spreadsheet, flag repeats. Ugly, but works.

Here's the prompt skeleton for the reading step:

You are analyzing a company's public hiring data to determine whether they are in, or entering, a buying window for [PRODUCT_CATEGORY].

INPUT

[N] days of job postings for {company}: title, first-posted date, repost count, full description text. Optionally: headcount trend, recent funding, tech stack mentions.

STEP 1 — DETECT SIGNALS (check each independently)

*   REPEAT_POSTING: same or near-identical role posted [3+] times in [90] days

→ broken: [retention leak they haven't named]

→ they buy: [engagement tooling, comp benchmarking]

*   FIRST_HIRE: first-ever [FUNCTION] role, no incumbent findable

→ broken: no owner, no process

→ they buy: [category], fast — no procurement, founder decides

*   STALE_ROLE: role live [60+] days, unfilled

→ broken: sourcing

→ they buy: [assessment, sourcing tech]

*   MIGRATION: "[INCUMBENT_PLATFORM] implementation/migration" in a JD

→ broken: switching cost already accepted

→ they buy: every adjacent tool in the category, [X]-day window

*   [CUSTOM_SIGNAL]: [your vertical's tell]

STEP 2 — DISQUALIFY BEFORE SCORING

*   Ghost jobs: evergreen postings, no edits [180+] days

*   Staffing agencies / RPOs posting on the company's behalf

*   Duplicates across boards (count as one)

*   Outside [GEO] / [HEADCOUNT_RANGE] / [INDUSTRY_FILTER]

STEP 3 — MAP SIGNAL TO BUYER

*   REPEAT_POSTING → [hiring manager] · FIRST_HIRE → [founder/CEO]

*   STALE_ROLE → [Head of TA] · MIGRATION → [HRIS owner / CPO]

STEP 4 — CALIBRATE

*   Every signal needs verbatim evidence quoted from the posting.

*   Confidence below 60 → NONE.

*   Prefer false negatives. Ad budget is expensive; a smaller

cleaner list beats a bigger dirty one.

RESPOND ONLY WITH JSON

{"company":"","signals":[{"type":"","evidence":"verbatim quote",

"confidence":0}],"diagnosis":"","buying_window":"NOW|NEXT_90_DAYS|NONE",

"target_persona":"","recommended_angle":"","disqualifiers_found":[]}

Backtest it against your last 15 closed-won accounts before trusting it.

Then the list-building exercise: Apollo, BetterContact or similar to find the right decision-makers, their LinkedIn, their emails. Upload the list to LinkedIn as a matched audience.

Match rate matters: if yours is under roughly 70%, there are tools built for exactly this like Clay Ads and ContactLevel (industry average company match runs 29–62%, per Dreamdata). Matching takes about 48 hours.

![Image 4](https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,quality=80,format=auto,onerror=redirect/uploads/asset/file/cb4bf5ec-95a9-48bf-96cf-18fb28bd626c/image.png?t=1788454352)

## Step 4: Classify where companies are in the buying journey to create the “they discovered you” feeling.

Title: The availability heuristic: 7 ways Google Ads can steer your decisions

URL Source: https://searchengineland.com/the-availability-heuristic-7-ways-google-ads-can-steer-your-decisions-487769

Published Time: 2026-09-11T13:00:00+00:00

Markdown Content:
Experienced Google advertisers know where to find the data that’s essential to optimization and insight. But many novices aren’t even aware of the layers they’re missing.

And misleading information often replaces hidden information — at least in the current context. As a result, many advertisers find themselves unwittingly accepting platform-friendly narratives.

If you don’t fall into the novice category or neglect your account(s), why should this matter to you? Second-order effects.

If you’re Advertiser A, doing a pretty darn competent job, the shortcomings and neglect in accounts managed by Advertisers B, C, D, E, and F can cause all kinds of auction anomalies that can rattle your cage, too.

Hopefully, more advertisers will discover that the temptations inside Google Ads are bad for their financial health. I’ll walk you through my biggest concerns, why advertisers are so susceptible, and what to do about them.

## How Google Ads leverages the availability heuristic

The [availability heuristic](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/0010028573900339) describes what happens when well-meaning people are swayed by readily available information.

Take transportation safety, for example. Hearing vivid anecdotes about plane crashes could lead to overlooking the fact that, statistically, the aviation industry is safe overall. That’s how journalism, and perhaps our penchant for narrative, tend to work.

But with Google Ads, Google itself pushes narratives directly into the platform. This makes platform-friendly ideas more visible to you as you spend your ad budget.

Platform-focused storytelling even determines the naming of features and campaign types. For instance, names like [Performance Max](https://searchengineland.com/google-performance-max-431821), [AI Max](https://searchengineland.com/ai-max-for-search-everything-you-need-to-know-462923), [Smart Bidding](https://searchengineland.com/your-guide-to-google-ads-smart-bidding-453765), and [Demand Gen](https://searchengineland.com/google-demand-gen-campaigns-migration-and-best-practices-433014) might be there to sway you. There’s an awful lot in a name if it can influence your budget allocation decisions.

What are some of the most common examples of manipulative, overly available, or hard-to-find information in Google Ads? Let’s look at seven in detail.

[See exactly how your competitors win. Uncover the keywords, ads, landing pages, and strategies driving your competitors’ paid search success—and find your next opportunity to outperform them. Analyze your competitors](https://www.semrush.com/analytics/traffic/paid-search?utm_campaign=ic_sel_0101ppc&utm_source=searchengineland.com&utm_medium=overlay&onboarding=off)
## 1. Dashboard views

At the account or campaign level, many advertisers might accept the default key performance indicators (KPIs) on the dashboard, including comparative data for the previous period. This can be suboptimal for a couple of reasons.

First, why compare to the previous period when, for most companies, year-over-year (YoY) is the more salient comparison? YoY comparisons help avoid faulty comparisons due to seasonal fluctuations. Second, aggregate impressions and clicks probably mean far less than metrics like revenue and return on ad spend (ROAS).

![Image 1: Passive account management means never changing the featured dashboard metrics.](blob:http://localhost/c60ab822347f0ad1f68d5754d36d2ea0)

_\_Passive account management means never changing the featured dashboard metrics.\__

**_Dig deeper:_**[**_Are you being manipulated by Google Ads?_**](https://searchengineland.com/google-ads-manipulation-432089)

## 2. Columns

Similarly, the default dashboard columns favor noise over signal. At times, it seems like Google has packed the display with columns you don’t need.

For my purposes, I want to look at key metrics such as clicks, click-through rate (CTR), conversion value, conversion value divided by cost, and cost per click (CPC).

At the earliest opportunity, learn which metrics are essential to your account and which you don’t need. Then, tailor the column selection through _Columns > Modify._

![Image 2: Pick a column, any column](blob:http://localhost/1c6277c374f929be387d0606ffaa8fd6)

_Pick a column, any column_

But know that naming tricks lurk in the available columns, too. Absolute top and top impression share (IS) might be handy competitive metrics, while search lost top IS (rank) probably isn’t. Anything that makes me feel restless and worried instead of calmly analytical is likely something I’d be better off not looking at.

## 3. Rows

As you check your dashboard, you might notice that your preferred number of rows displayed (typically 50 or 100) sometimes reverts to the minimum of 10.

Since pagination compromises optimization, some advertisers may work on only a couple of campaigns or view only a couple of pages’ worth of data before they decide to move on to something else.

The more friction there is, the more unoptimized account sections will fester. For example, if you inherited an unwieldy account with too many campaigns, you’ll need to ditch the status quo and figure out how to consolidate. Financial performance almost always improves.

Get the newsletter search marketers rely on.

* * *

## 4. Optimization Score and recommendations

Google constantly nudges advertisers to pore through and accept categorized account recommendations. Take this reminder, for example:

![Image 3: The lightbulb is there to illuminate what Google wants you to do.](blob:http://localhost/8938e81716cc39da6c369e726c5056e3)

_The lightbulb is there to illuminate what Google wants you to do_

It includes two suggestions to remove redundant keywords and enable Display Expansion. Neither is going to help much. And the latter is almost certainly going to hurt your performance — unless you’re under threat of losing your job if you fail to spend a bloated budget by a certain deadline, regardless of performance.

**_Dig deeper: [4 Google Ads settings and recommendations worth a closer look](https://searchengineland.com/google-ads-settings-recommendations-closer-look-484156)_**

From a performance perspective, surface-level account management consistently fails. Say you have a campaign-level ROAS target your predecessor set at 350%. You keep pushing it higher to achieve what you hope will be a tighter campaign with lower spend and higher ROI.

But performance doesn’t budge. So, you panic and eventually limit the daily budget, pause the campaign, or blame made-up economic headwinds.

Meanwhile, the ad group-level targets were set to a variety of levels between 210% and 260%. They overrode the campaign-level setting you kept adjusting. You’ll never find out if you don’t crack open that campaign and drill down.

## 6. Search query reporting

Novice advertisers don’t know much, if anything, about keyword match types. Many novices don’t distinguish between keywords in their account and the user queries that mapped to those keywords. And they don’t know where to find search term reporting, either.

Here are a few categories of ill-mapped queries that advertisers should add as negative search terms in a particular ad group, campaign, or account:

*   Purely navigational brand searches that drive up apparent ROI for niche acquisition keywords.
*   Single-word queries (like “office”) in a category where you sell specific products.
*   Brands and products you don’t sell.
*   Competitor names if they shouldn’t be there.
*   Brands and products that should map to other parts of the account.

[Every click they win is a customer you lose. See where competitors are investing, which keywords drive their results, and how to capture more of the market. See who’s stealing your traffic](https://www.semrush.com/analytics/traffic/paid-search?utm_campaign=ic_sel_0102ppc&utm_source=searchengineland.com&utm_medium=overlay&onboarding=off)
## 7. Conversion counts

Figure out your KPIs, pick the primary one, and keep a few secondary ones on your dashboard for monitoring and background information. If you want deeper dives or multiple primary KPIs for additional precision, you could either use Google Analytics or import a couple of those goals into Google Ads and designate them as primary and secondary.

Notice how it’s already getting messy?

If you inherit a mature account, the reality might be much more byzantine. A multitude of account managers and stakeholders have made choices, and now the logic is all over the map.

The first thing you’ll want to do is be sure no one has set virtually identical KPIs as primary. Sadly, this is a fairly common practice.

Then clean up the remaining conversions. Take mildly valuable (but only directionally helpful) conversion events like store visits or even sought directions to the store. If they happen infrequently and provide valuable insights, directional KPIs help with optimization. If they’re too frequent and skew real revenue feedback, there’s nothing wrong with removing them entirely.

**_Dig deeper:_**[**_Outsmarting Google Ads: Insider strategies to navigate changes like a pro_**](https://searchengineland.com/outsmarting-google-ads-insider-strategies-453124)

## Know the tactics to avoid the platform’s influence

I’ve covered seven examples, but there are many others. As an advertiser, you’re playing a shell game where most advertisers are regularly influenced purely by what they think they see.

Your superpower? The operator of the shell game still lets you lift the shells, some of the time.

Title: 9 Successful Media Pitch Examples for Every Type of Campaign

URL Source: https://www.buzzstream.com/blog/media-pitch-examples/

Published Time: 2026-09-09T14:17:11+00:00

Markdown Content:
Table of Contents

*   [What is a Media Pitch?](https://www.buzzstream.com/blog/media-pitch-examples/#What_is_a_Media_Pitch "What is a Media Pitch?")
*   [How to Write a Media Pitch, Broadly](https://www.buzzstream.com/blog/media-pitch-examples/#How_to_Write_a_Media_Pitch_Broadly "How to Write a Media Pitch, Broadly")
*   [1. Survey Study Pitch Example](https://www.buzzstream.com/blog/media-pitch-examples/#1_Survey_Study_Pitch_Example "1. Survey Study Pitch Example")
*   [2. Proprietary Research or Data Pitch](https://www.buzzstream.com/blog/media-pitch-examples/#2_Proprietary_Research_or_Data_Pitch "2. Proprietary Research or Data Pitch")
*   [3. The City / Regional Index Study Pitch](https://www.buzzstream.com/blog/media-pitch-examples/#3_The_City_Regional_Index_Study_Pitch "3. The City / Regional Index Study Pitch")
*   [4. Reactive Commentary Pitch](https://www.buzzstream.com/blog/media-pitch-examples/#4_Reactive_Commentary_Pitch "4. Reactive Commentary Pitch")
*   [5. Reactive Commentary (with tips)](https://www.buzzstream.com/blog/media-pitch-examples/#5_Reactive_Commentary_with_tips "5. Reactive Commentary (with tips)")
*   [6. Proactive Commentary Pitch](https://www.buzzstream.com/blog/media-pitch-examples/#6_Proactive_Commentary_Pitch "6. Proactive Commentary Pitch")
*   [7. Product Launch Announcement](https://www.buzzstream.com/blog/media-pitch-examples/#7_Product_Launch_Announcement "7. Product Launch Announcement")
*   [8. The Product Review Pitch](https://www.buzzstream.com/blog/media-pitch-examples/#8_The_Product_Review_Pitch "8. The Product Review Pitch")
*   [9. Product Roundup Inclusion](https://www.buzzstream.com/blog/media-pitch-examples/#9_Product_Roundup_Inclusion "9. Product Roundup Inclusion")
*   [Ask Yourself: Would I Cover This?](https://www.buzzstream.com/blog/media-pitch-examples/#Ask_Yourself_Would_I_Cover_This "Ask Yourself: Would I Cover This?")

*   **Answer “why now?” first** — tie your pitch to your own news, the season, or something already breaking.
*   **Skip forced personalizatio**n — only ~25% of pitches reference a journalist’s past coverage, and it can backfire.
*   **Give them everything to write the story**, not just enough to make them reply.
*   **Always ask for coverage** — 92% of pitches that land include a direct ask.
*   **Match the format to the outlet** — full release for local/trade, just the stat and a link for national.

There’s no such thing as a perfect [media pitch](https://www.buzzstream.com/blog/media-pitch/).

Every campaign is different.

And each pitch is built to deliver _specific_ information to a journalist.

To figure out what that information is, I dug into thousands of successful emails our users sent to see what they all had in common.

I crunched reply rates, open rates, and the actual pitch copy behind the numbers to understand the traits of a successful pitch.

I even asked some journalists which they prefer and why.

So, here are 9 media pitch templates that you can count on for different types of PR outreach.

## What is a Media Pitch?

A media pitch is a targeted email offering a journalist a story, source, product, dataset, or other material relevant to their coverage and audience.

And I say email specifically because [Cision’s State of the Media](https://www.cision.com/resources/guides-and-reports/sotm/) calls out email as the main preference for outreach.

(No sliding into DMs.)

Before we get into the examples, let’s look at the broad building blocks of a media pitch.

## How to Write a Media Pitch, Broadly

Although I said in the intro that every media pitch is different (it is), pitches share some common elements.

Based on my years of experience, BuzzStream users, and conversations with journalists, here’s how to write one, broadly:

### 1. Lead with the finding/news

Your first line has a lot of work to do, but mainly it needs to **catch their attention.**

There are a few ways to do this, which can be solved by answering the following questions:

**Answer “why now?”:**

As I wrote about in my [“why now” piece](https://www.buzzstream.com/blog/why-now/), every journalist needs to understand why they should cover your story right now.

Tying your pitch to a seasonal trend, an event, or breaking news all gives the journalist a reason to act on your pitch now.

**Answer “why them?”:**

Your pitch should be immediately relevant to the journalist and their audience.

In some cases (only about 25% based on my dataset), PR pros reference a journalist’s existing coverage to answer “why them”.

Lines like “since you wrote about X topic” or “I saw your piece on X,” carry a big risk if they aren’t immediately relevant to the story you pitch.

They can be negative if they are forced, shallow, or inauthentic (e.g., “I saw your post this morning and really loved it!”).

I’d save them for reactive pitches, where you are calling out a relevant article they wrote that you are reacting to, and instances where you are genuinely sharing a very similar story to the one they covered.

### 2. Say who you are

In any case, the journalist needs to know who you are: the brand pitching the product, the expert commentator, the person running the study, etc.

This will not only put things into context, but it will also help them trust you.

### 3. Give all the info needed to cover

This is the meat of the pitch.

Here, share whatever information the journalist needs to cover your story.

This includes key information like:

*   Data
*   Quotes
*   Event information
*   Pricing
*   Launch times/dates

If you are unclear whether you are giving them enough information, PR pro [Hannah Smith](https://worderist.com/) suggested this helpful exercise in a [podcast episode](https://www.buzzstream.com/blog/pitching-to-journalists-podcast/):

Ask yourself, ‘_based on what I’ve written in my pitch, can the journalist write a story, or will they need to reply and ask for more?’_

If the answer is no, then you probably need to give them more info.

### 4. Ask for coverage

Based on my data, about **92% of the templates include an ask.**

Lines like:

*   “Is this something you’d consider covering?”
*   “Any questions”
*   “Let me know what you think”

Most journalists will tell you that it doesn’t matter; if they are interested, they will reply, but I always err on the side of including it.

### 5. Include a press release (sometimes)

In my analysis of [digital PR in the UK vs US](https://www.buzzstream.com/blog/us-vs-uk-digital-pr/), I’ve found that pasting a full press release within an email pitch is a very UK-centric approach.

My take on this is that it comes down to who you are reaching out to.

A local or trade editor who’s going to run something close to verbatim wants the release ready to lift, so they don’t have to email you back asking for it.

A national columnist writing 800 words of original copy around your one good stat doesn’t want 1,200 words of release; they probably want the number and a link to check it.

OK, with those out of the way, let’s get to media pitch examples and templates.

These templates (except for one) are based on my research, but I’ve replaced topics and names and had AI help rewrite some of the findings/data to protect client and customer confidentiality.

## 1. Survey Study Pitch Example

Pitching data and research was the most-used digital PR strategy, according to our [State of Digital PR report](https://www.buzzstream.com/blog/state-of-digital-pr-2026/), so I’ll start here.

This is the pitch you send when you have original research you’re using to earn coverage.

### What to include

What to include

*   ✓ A sample size or scope.
*   ✓ 3-5 bulleted findings, not paragraphs.
*   ✓ A link to the full dataset, not an attachment.
*   ✓ At least one finding that runs counter to expectations.

### Example Pitch:

[Exclusive] 3 in 5 Remote Workers Have Never Met Their Manager in Person
Hi Priya,

Last week, Charge Research found that 90% of companies are pushing employees back to the office by Labor Day.

Fielder’s new study found that 3 in 5 remote workers have never met their managers face-to-face.

Fielder surveyed 1,204 full-time remote employees at US companies with 50+ staff to see how working relationships change when nobody’s ever met in person.

Key findings:

 – 71% have never met their manager in person

 – 34% report lower confidence their manager would advocate for them in layoffs

 – 1 in 4 say they’d turn down a return-to-office mandate (even if it meant finally meeting their manager)

View the full study: fielder.com/research/never-met-my-manager

Would you be interested in covering this? Happy to connect you with our Head of People Research for additional context.

Best,

 Theo

Copy to Clipboard

### Why it works

**“****Why now” comes first, but there’s a twist.**

The “why now” isn’t Fielder’s news at all; it’s hooking onto **another event.**

That’s one of my favorite moves: you don’t need a timely event of your own if you can attach to a conversation already happening.

(And yes, it does blur the lines into [newsjacking](https://www.buzzstream.com/blog/newsjacking/).)

**No personalization.**

There’s no “I saw your piece on…” here.

The [subject line](https://www.buzzstream.com/blog/how-to-write-subject-lines/) and the first two lines convey the relevance.

“ **Who you are” also reiterates the sample size.**

“Fielder surveyed 1,204 full-time remote employees at US companies with 50+ staff” puts the source and the survey scope in one sentence.

**The bullets add rather than repeat.**

The headline finding is already stated twice by this point, once in the subject line and the second sentence, so the bullets don’t need it again.

Instead, the bullets go deeper.

## 2. Proprietary Research or Data Pitch

Although survey data is technically proprietary data, I do think it changes a bit

### What to include:

What to include

*   ✓ A link to the data and asset/post (if applicable).
*   ✓ An expert comment on the topic.

This one is a real pitch that landed, sent to me by tech journalist [Jasper Hammil](https://www.linkedin.com/in/jasperhamill?originalSubdomain=uk) of [Machine](https://www.machine.news/).

Note: I haven’t actually changed much in this pitch (I even kept the British spellings!)

### Example Pitch:

RESEARCH: North Korea’s Lazarus group weaponised a zero-day exploit hidden in a job offer
Hi Jasper,

Check Point Research has uncovered the latest wave of ‘Operation Dream Job’, a long-running campaign by the DPRK-linked Lazarus group.

The North Korea-linked hacking group is running a defence industry recruitment scam so convincing it fooled Google itself: fake Lockheed Martin and Enveil job postings, SEO’d to the top of search results, that deliver a never-before-seen backdoor and a Windows zero-day (CVE-2026-68820, patched this week) capable of full SYSTEM takeover.

Every layer of the attack was “legitimate.”

The recruiter, the vendor’s website, the top Google result and even the servers relaying stolen data were all borrowed from real, trusted infrastructure.

In one case, Lazarus hijacked an already-compromised French company to spam out the campaign to new victims worldwide, weaponising one breach into the next.

The full research can be found here: [link to full research] and a high-level blog here: [link to blog]

Commenting on the research, Sergey Shykevich, Director, Threat Intelligence at Check Point Software, said: “What makes this campaign so dangerous is not only the zero-day vulnerability – but also how Lazarus wove legitimate, trusted infrastructure into every stage of the attack.

They hid in plain sight, behind top-ranked search results, real vendor branding, and the reputation of organisations they had already compromised. When the website, the download and the recruiter all appear authentic, the old advice to ‘spot the phishing link’ is no longer easily applicable.

Staying safe now means assuming that trust itself can be counterfeited: patch the moment updates land, verify software through official channels rather than search rankings, and extend zero-trust thinking to the legitimate-looking sites and partners we interact with every day.”

For any further information or to speak with Sergey, please get in touch.

Best,

Copy to Clipboard

### Why it works

I don’t have to guess on this one.

Here’s what Jasper told me in his own words:

_“I love this story in general: North Korea is using fake job offers to target the defense sector._

_And this was a great pitch because it’s urgent, subtly alarmist, and uses strong language like ‘weaponized’ in the headline._

_It manages to avoid FUD (fear, uncertainty, doubt) — which I know is very unpopular in security — while still being dramatic._

_The first line about ‘Operation Dream Job’ is so engaging and makes you want to read on. It then tells a very good story, with all the details in a few pars and a quote that’s technical enough for specialists — but still exciting._

_Sure, this is an agency that specializes in security, but it’s still rare for PR folks to squeeze so much information into such a short space, whilst making the content readable and ensuring we click the research to learn more. The perfect security pitch.”_

Let’s dig into what he’s saying because it basically maps to my framework exactly:

**Leading with the finding.**

Jasper singles out the first line, naming “Operation Dream Job” as the thing that made him keep reading.

**Explains “why now?”**

It mentions that the security threat was “patched this week”.

**Mentions who****_you_****are.**

Check Point Research is named in the first five words.

**The info they need to write it.**

He does a great job of compressing the full narrative into a few paragraphs, plus a quote.

Jasper said it explicitly says it got him to click through, which is the whole job.

## 3. The City / Regional Index Study Pitch

The [city index study](https://www.buzzstream.com/blog/city-study/)is a real workhorse of the digital PR industry.

This is where you typically focus on the best and worst cities/regions and pitch on that angle.

### What to include

What to include

*   ✓ The local result in the subject line.
*   ✓ A bit on the methodology.
*   ✓ An offer of a dataset or link to it.

### Example Pitch

Hull named UK’s best city for first-time gardeners
Hi Faye,

With the first frost-free weekend finally behind us, research shows more people are starting to garden this spring than at any point since 2021.

But which cities actually give a beginner the best shot at keeping something alive?

To answer that, Greenhouse Direct’s Bloom Index 2026 examined average garden size, growing-season length, soil quality, and allotment access across 60 UK cities.

Hull came out on top!

Key findings:

 – Hull’s frost-free growing season now runs 217 days, longer than Bristol’s

 – Top-10 cities have allotment waiting lists averaging 14 months shorter than the national average

 – London ranks 52nd of 60, despite topping national searches for “how to start a garden”

Here is early access to the full dataset.

If you’re interested in covering this and/or would like to connect with our CEO, Frank Simpson, for an interview, I’m happy to connect you.

Many thanks,

 Adam

Copy to Clipboard

### Why it works

**Why now is answered in sentence one.**

Most city indexes have no real timeliness to them, but most can borrow one from the [PR calendar](https://www.buzzstream.com/blog/pr-calendar/), like hiking season, school holidays, the first warm weekend, back-to-school, etc.

The best-performing versions I looked at all did this.

One opened with “Summer is here, and that means it’s HIKING SEASON!” Another tied a beach ranking to the peak of the school summer holidays.

**The setup question keeps them reading.**

Not a necessity, but three of the five strongest city pitches I read used it.

It keeps readers reading and can even inspire headlines phrased as what they’re already wondering.

**“Why them” is the geo hook.**

This is the part people get wrong about city studies. Local journalists will mainly care about their own city, not the national angle.

**The methodology sentence is there.**

“Examined average garden size, growing-season length, soil quality, and allotment access across 60 UK cities.”

## 4. Reactive Commentary Pitch

[Reactive commentary pitches](https://www.buzzstream.com/blog/reactive-pr-us-podcast/) typically have no study behind it, just some quotes.

You’re typically offering access to a qualified persona with something useful to say about something that’s happening or about to happen.

(Some also like to also include tips so the journalist can write an entire article.)

### What to include

What to include

*   ✓ The news event and its timing in the first sentence.
*   ✓ The credentials of the commenter.
*   ✓ A fresh, counterintuitive, or otherwise interesting quote.

### Example Pitch:

Expert comment: what today’s interest rate hold means for first-time buyers
Hi Grace,

With the Bank of England holding rates at 4.25% today, I wanted to share an expert comment from Owen Baptiste, Mortgage Director at Harrow & Vale.

Owen has spent nine years advising first-time buyers through three separate rate cycles, and has arranged over 4,000 first-time mortgages.

On what today’s hold means in practice, Owen says:

“The rate hold itself won’t move much for buyers already mid-application, but it does mean lenders have less pressure to sharpen their fixed-rate deals this month.

Anyone hoping a cut today translates into a cheaper five-year fix by summer should recalibrate.

We’re more likely looking at autumn.

The bigger risk right now isn’t the rate itself.

Now, it’s buyers assuming a cut and stretching their affordability ahead of a decision that hasn’t happened yet.”

Happy to arrange an interview or provide further comment.

Best,

 Hana

Copy to Clipboard

### Why it works

**“Why now” is immediate.**

“With the Bank of England holding rates at 4.25% **today** .” That’s it.

Reactive comments have some of the shortest shelf lives of anything on this list.

**The credential is specific.**

“Nine years,” “three rate cycles,” “over 4,000 first-time mortgages.”

It tells her precisely what he’s qualified to say about this story.

**The quote provides a new angle.**

It makes an argument: the real risk isn’t the rate; it’s buyers pricing in a cut that hasn’t happened. It isn’t obvious; thus, it’s valuable for a journalist.

### The one thing that separates good commentary from filler

Across every commentary pitch I read, strong or weak, the difference came down to a single question: **Could anyone else have said this?**

My conversations with [Madeleine Dykes on reactive PR in the US](https://www.buzzstream.com/blog/reactive-pr-us-podcast/) and [Leah Daly on reactive PR in the UK](https://www.buzzstream.com/blog/reactive-pr-podcast/) really outline this well.

That’s the whole game in this format.

## 5. Reactive Commentary (with tips)

This builds on the previous example: you provide a quote, but you add extra value with included tips.

As I mentioned in the beginning, this is a very UK-centric approach typically found in publications like the [Daily Mail](https://www.dailymail.com/lifestyle/article-3398445/Which-cosy-coat-keeps-chill-FEMAIL-finds-wearing-stay-warm-cold.html).

### What to include

What to include

*   ✓ The news event and its timing in the first sentence.
*   ✓ The credentials of the commenter.
*   ✓ A fresh, counterintuitive, or otherwise interesting quote.
*   ✓ Tips the journalist can use to write the story.

### Example Pitch:

Pharmacist warns hay fever sufferers as pollen count hits season high
Hi Emily,

Google searches for “hay fever relief” are up 61% in the past seven days, and more people are dealing with symptoms right now than at any point this year.

Standard antihistamines are often not enough on their own, and a lot of people double up in ways that don’t help.

Nadia Fenwick, Superintendent Pharmacist at Clearwell Pharmacy, has spent eleven years advising on seasonal allergy treatment and reviews over 200 hay fever consultations a week during peak season.

She’s shared what to do differently when the count is this high, and the three mistakes she sees most often.

Her full guidance is below — happy to send over anything else you need from Nadia.

Best,

 Charity

—

Five things to do differently when the pollen count is very high

1. Take your antihistamine before you need it, not when symptoms start.

If you know you’re sensitive, start a fortnight before the season really gets going rather than waiting for the first bad day.”
